section.t: Pre-prepare digest semantics: For a bft_preprepare message, digest is SHA-256(ring_id || view || sequence || QUIP-CBOR-encode(operation)), where ring_id is the 32-byte ring identifier, view and sequence are encoded as 8-byte big-endian unsigned integers, and || denotes byte concatenation. Witnesses MUST recompute this digest from the received fields and reject the message with E_BFT_FAILURE (error code 0x0B) if it does not match.

New-view prepared messages: Each entry in prepared_messages is a complete bft_preprepare message as it would appear on the wire, including the primary's signature. It is not a digest. The new primary re-proposes these messages, and witnesses re-verify the primary's signature.
State-transfer signing payload: For bft_state_transfer, the ring_signature covers the message array with the ring_signature element removed, encoded with QUIP-CBOR. This is consistent with .

ul.li: A quorum is 5 of 7 witnesses (VIEW_CHANGE_QUORUM = 5).
A bft_new_view message MUST contain at least VIEW_CHANGE_QUORUM (5) valid view-change messages.
A checkpoint MUST be signed by at least VIEW_CHANGE_QUORUM (5) witnesses to be considered stable.

li.t: A state transfer MUST include a RingSignature that is either:

ul.li: 5 individual Ed25519 signatures from distinct witnesses, ordered by canonical NodeId with corresponding signer list, or
A FROST aggregate signature from 5 of 7 witnesses.
Recipients MUST validate the quorum threshold before accepting any state transfer.

section.t: Ring Signature Validation: Recipients of a bft_state_transfer MUST validate the RingSignature by either:

ul.li: For IndividualRingSig: verifying each signature against the corresponding witness's public key (matched by position in the signers list) and the state digest.
For FrostRingSig: verifying the aggregate signature against the group public key and the state digest.

ol.li: Primary proposes operation (PRE-PREPARE)
Witnesses verify and respond (PREPARE) — need 5 of 7
Witnesses commit to prepare (PRECOMMIT) — need 5 of 7
Witnesses finalize (COMMIT) — need 5 of 7
Operation is applied to DVV

section.t: View Changes: If the primary is suspected faulty, witnesses initiate a view change. Ring membership is ordered by canonical NodeId order (bytewise lexicographic over the 32-byte NodeId). The primary for view v is the member at position v mod |R| in that order. This is a deterministic assignment: every honest witness computes the same primary for a given view number from the same ring membership, without coordination. Provided the ring membership is unchanged, a view change from view v to view v + 1 advances the primary to the next member in canonical order, wrapping at the end. When membership changes between views, v mod |R| still determines the primary but the "next member" relationship may not hold across the change.

When |R| < WITNESS_COUNT (for example, in DEGRADED mode), the ordering is applied to the reachable members of the ring, not the full nominal ring. Implementations MUST agree on the reachable subset before applying the rotation; disagreement about membership is handled as a view-change failure and forces a further view bump.
The view change includes quorum certificates for prepared messages and the latest stable checkpoint to ensure safety across view changes.
Consensus Requirements: Operations in QUIP fall into two categories:

tr.td: Key rotations, revocations, witness membership changes, resource ownership transfers
Full BFT (5 of 7 witnesses) — MUST NOT proceed in DEGRADED mode
Applied immediately; BFT only on conflict detection

section.t: Optimistic Execution Eligibility: An operation is eligible for optimistic execution if:

ul.li: It does not change the membership of a witness ring
It does not involve key rotation or revocation
It does not transfer ownership of a resource
The peer has KT_VERIFIED status for the NodeId

section.t: Peers with KT_PENDING status MAY issue writes, but such writes are NOT eligible for optimistic execution; they MUST await BFT confirmation. This is an intentional liveness trade-off for new peers.

If an optimistic write later conflicts with another write, the DVV merge algorithm resolves the conflict deterministically. The witness ring is only involved if the conflict cannot be resolved causally.
Optimistic Mode: For eligible operations (approximately 95% of writes), peers use optimistic execution:

ul.li: Write is applied to DVV immediately
Witnesses verify in the background
BFT consensus runs only when conflicts are detected

section.t: This provides low latency for normal operations. See for performance expectations.

section.name: Operations
section.t: An Operation is a CBOR item with the following properties:

ul.li: Its encoding MUST be canonical QUIP-CBOR (). The signing payload of bft_preprepare includes the operation as encoded on the wire; non-canonical operations will cause verification failures.

An operation MUST have a kind — a text string identifying what class of state transition it represents. The kinds currently defined by this specification are "key_rotation", "revocation", "witness_membership_change", and "resource_ownership_transfer". Applications MAY define additional kinds.
An operation MUST have a subject — the state it acts on. Two operations with different subjects never conflict.

An operation MUST define, as part of its application-layer specification, a conflict relation with other operations of the same kind. Two operations of the same kind conflict if applying both produces a state that would not have been produced by applying either alone.
Witnesses MUST NOT interpret operation payloads beyond the kind and subject fields. Application-layer conflict detection is performed by the operation's registered handler, not by the ring itself.

Operation size: operations SHOULD be at most 4 KiB. Larger operations MAY be accepted but SHOULD be rate-limited or rejected on a per-ring basis. Implementations MAY advertise a per-ring operation size cap in the ring's membership announcement.

section.t: The CDDL for Operation is defined with the BFT messages above:

section.name: BFT Checkpointing
section.t: Checkpointing is an OPTIONAL extension that enables stable state truncation, recovery, and state transfer. It SHOULD be enabled for long-running witness rings.

ol.li: When a witness's sequence number reaches a multiple of CHECKPOINT_INTERVAL (default 100), it sends a bft_checkpoint message to the ring.
Witnesses collect checkpoint messages until 5-of-7 have been received for the same state digest.
The ring stores the stable checkpoint digest and sequence number.
Checkpoints enable view-change messages to include a stable checkpoint, preventing long replay attacks.
A witness that falls behind can request bft_state_transfer from peers with the stable checkpoint.

figure.artwork: CHECKPOINT_INTERVAL = 100 ; Checkpoint every 100 consensus rounds VIEW_CHANGE_QUORUM = 5 ; Quorum size for view changes and checkpoints

section.t: State Transfer: A witness that has fallen behind can request state transfer from the ring:

ol.li: The lagging witness sends a bft_state_transfer request containing its latest known checkpoint sequence.
A witness with the stable checkpoint responds with the state and a RingSignature (5 of 7 witnesses).
The lagging witness verifies the ring signature and applies the state.
The lagging witness resumes participation from the checkpoint.

section.t: State Format: The state field is an opaque byte string whose internal structure is defined by the application that uses the BFT ring. This specification does not mandate a serialization. The following requirements apply:

ul.li: The checkpoint_digest field MUST be the SHA-256 of the state bytes as transmitted.

The state bytes MUST be deterministically decodable by any implementation of the same application, so that a lagging witness from a different codebase can reconstruct the ring's state without ambiguity. Applications SHOULD define their state serialization in a companion specification.

At minimum, the state SHOULD encode the DVV the ring is tracking, the current view and sequence number, and any operations applied since the last stable checkpoint. The choice of encoding is the application's.

A recipient that cannot decode the state MUST reject the transfer with E_BFT_FAILURE (error code 0x0B) rather than apply a state it cannot validate. Silently accepting an unparseable state is a protocol violation.

section.t: Checkpointing is recommended for deployments with high churn or long-running rings.

section.name: Key Rotation
section.t: Only the NodeId itself can sign a key rotation. No domain or external authority can revoke or rotate keys.

figure.artwork: KeyRotation = [ "quip-v1", "key_rotation", old_NodeId: bytes .size 32, new_NodeId: bytes .size 32, timestamp: uint, signature: bytes .size 64 ; Signed by old_NodeId ]

section.t: Witness Requirement: A new key MUST be witnessed by 2+ existing witnesses before KT_VERIFIED status transfers.
Discontinuous Identity Mode: Users MAY break the rotation chain permanently:

figure.artwork: Discontinuity = [ "quip-v1", "identity_discontinuity", old_NodeId: bytes .size 32, new_NodeId: bytes .size 32, timestamp: uint, export_token: bytes, ; Optional data portability proof signature: bytes .size 64 ]

ul.li: No cryptographic link between old and new identities
KT_VERIFIED status does NOT transfer
Old NodeId MUST be tombstoned

section.name: Sequence Number Reset
section.t: If a node loses its sequence number state, it MUST publish a seq_reset attestation.

figure.artwork: SeqReset = [ "quip-v1", "seq_reset", NodeId: bytes .size 32, last_known_seq: uint, timestamp: uint, ; Unix milliseconds signature: bytes .size 64 ]
MAX_REPLAY_WINDOW = 300000 ; 300 seconds (5 minutes), expressed in Unix ; milliseconds to match the `timestamp` ; field used throughout this document

section.t: Acceptance Condition: Given last_seen_time (Unix milliseconds) from this NodeId:

ul.li: If timestamp < last_seen_time - MAX_REPLAY_WINDOW: MUST reject
If timestamp > now + MAX_REPLAY_WINDOW: MUST reject (future timestamp)
Otherwise: MUST accept

section.t: MAX_REPLAY_WINDOW is a fixed protocol constant expressed in Unix milliseconds, consistent with every other timestamp field in this document, and MUST NOT be modified by implementations.

Replay Window Security: The two-sided check enforces the clock skew assumption (A6 in ). Messages with timestamps more than 5 minutes in the future are rejected to prevent attackers from exploiting unbounded future timestamps.

section.name: Witness Ring Constants: Rationale
section.t: This section provides the rationale for the witness ring constants specified in . The constants are derived from a specific adversary model and engineering trade-offs.

Adversary Model: We assume an adversary that can compromise up to 2 witnesses in any ring. This is consistent with a Byzantine fault tolerance threshold of f=2, which requires at least 3f+1 = 7 witnesses. The adversary is assumed to have:

ul.li: Computational resources sufficient to generate NodeIds that are XOR-close to a target (subject to the cost analysis in )
The ability to maintain adversarial nodes online for extended periods
No ability to compromise the target's private key
No ability to control 4+ witnesses in a ring simultaneously
BFT threshold: 3f+1 with f=2 yields 7 witnesses. This tolerates 2 Byzantine faults while maintaining liveness (need 5 of 7 for consensus).

f=2 justification: Controlling 3+ witnesses in a Kademlia ring requires finding 3 XOR-close NodeIds. The cost increases exponentially as the attacker attempts to place multiple nodes within the target's nearest-neighbor set. This analysis suggests that controlling 3+ witnesses becomes increasingly difficult as network size and witness diversity increase; however, the exact cost depends on deployment parameters.
Alternative considered: f=1 (5 witnesses) would tolerate only 1 fault, which is insufficient for a global adversarial network where coordinated attacks are possible.

Alternative considered: f=3 (9 witnesses) would increase overhead without improving security against the assumed adversary. The additional 2 witnesses add 29% more overhead (2/7) while providing no additional fault tolerance against the assumed adversary.

Security: Limits the duration of any successful ring takeover to a single epoch and forces all witnesses (including adversarial ones) to re-announce their membership daily. This creates operational friction and periodic churn, preventing long-term compromise of a witness ring. Note that in this version, rotation does not force an attacker to re-grind qualifying NodeIds (see for details and for potential nonce-binding enhancements).
Availability: Long enough that witnesses are stable and available, reducing churn and connection overhead.
Operational precedent: Matches common DNS TTL practices (24h) and certificate validity periods (24h-7d).
Alternative considered: 12-hour rotation would increase security but also increase overhead and churn. 48-hour rotation would reduce overhead but increase the window for compromise.
Latency: 7 witnesses require 5 responses for consensus, balancing fault tolerance and latency.
Bandwidth: 7 witnesses generate O(7) messages per consensus round, which is manageable for most deployments.
Implementation complexity: A fixed constant (7) is simpler to implement than a variable number of witnesses.

section.t: Future Flexibility: While version 1 fixes these constants, future versions MAY consider:

ul.li: Negotiable witness counts (e.g., 5 for low-power devices, 9 for high-security environments)
Configurable rotation intervals (e.g., 12h for faster churn, 48h for stability)
Nonce-bound rotation to cryptographically bind witnesses to epochs (see )

section.t: The version 1 constants are considered sufficient for the adversary model described in this section. Future work may provide more flexible mechanisms.

section.name: Gossip-Based Revocation
section.t: QUIP uses gossip-based revocation with no central list or authority.

figure.artwork: RevocationNotice = [ "quip-v1", "revocation", violator: NodeId, timestamp: uint, evidence: bytes, reporter: NodeId, signature: bytes .size 64 ]

ul.li: 5+ valid revocation notices from distinct reporters
Each notice MUST be validated
Once tombstoned, the key loses all KT_VERIFIED status

section.t: No central revocation list. Each witness maintains its own tombstone set.

section.name: Content Governance Primitives
section.t: This section defines protocol-level primitives that enable content governance applications (e.g., copyright enforcement, "right to be forgotten," content moderation). The primitives are designed to be flexible and application-agnostic; specific policies, algorithms, and evidence requirements are left to applications.

Note: The primitives defined in this section are OPTIONAL application-layer conventions, not protocol-enforced guarantees. A QUIP implementation that does not support governance primitives remains fully protocol-compliant. Support is advertised via the governance capability bit ().

Witnesses perform only syntactic validation (signatures, timestamps, quotas). They MUST NOT judge the semantic correctness of application-defined claims (e.g., whether a DMCA claim is valid). Applications MUST define their own evidence rules.

section.name: Trusted CID Registration
section.t: A Trusted CID (tCID) is a CID that has been registered as a reference for a specific work. Registration creates a binding between the cryptographic CID and application-defined metadata (e.g., perceptual hashes, ownership claims).

figure.artwork: TrustedCIDRegistration = [ "quip-v1", "register_tcid", cid: CIDOrV1, ; Cryptographic CID of the content app_metadata: { * tstr => any }, ; Application-defined metadata owner: NodeId, ; Owner or authorized agent timestamp: uint, ; Unix milliseconds signature: bytes .size 64 ; Signed by owner NodeId ]

section.t: The app_metadata field MAY contain:

ul.li: Perceptual hashes (pHash, aHash, dHash, AcoustID, etc.)
Title, author, description
Copyright registration numbers
Links to external evidence
Hash algorithm used (0 = SHA-256, 1 = BLAKE3)
Identifier format (0 = raw CID, 1 = CIDv1)
Any other application-defined metadata

section.t: Verification: The CID in the registration MUST match the content referenced. Implementations MAY verify application-defined metadata (e.g., that perceptual hashes are consistent with the content).
Delegation: The owner MAY delegate governance authority to other NodeIds:

figure.artwork: DelegationCertificate = [ "quip-v1", "delegation", trusted_cid: CIDOrV1, delegate: NodeId, permissions: uint .bits, ; Application-defined permission bits valid_from: uint, valid_until: uint, owner_sig: bytes .size 64 ]

section.name: Content Quarantine
section.t: Quarantine is a protocol-level state where a CID is marked as undiscoverable through DHT queries. Quarantined CIDs remain addressable by exact CID lookup but MUST NOT be returned in resource queries, DHT searches, or any discovery mechanism.

figure.artwork:
QuarantineRequest = [ "quip-v1", "quarantine", trusted_cid: CIDOrV1, affected_cids: [* CIDOrV1], ; CIDs to quarantine reason: tstr, ; Application-defined reason app_data: { * tstr => any }, ; Application-defined evidence timestamp: uint, requestor: NodeId, signature: bytes .size 64 ; Signed by requestor ]
QuarantineNotice = [ "quip-v1", "quarantine_notice", trusted_cid: CIDOrV1, affected_cids: [* CIDOrV1], reason: tstr, timestamp: uint, valid_until: uint, ; 0 = permanent ring_signature: RingSignature ; Signed by witness ring (5 of 7) ]

section.t: Quarantine Effect: Quarantine is an advisory discoverability filter, not a deletion or access-control mechanism. Quarantined CIDs:

ul.li: MUST NOT be returned in query_resource responses
MUST NOT be discoverable via the DHT
MAY still be accessible via exact CID lookup (if the user knows the exact CID)
SHOULD be tagged as "quarantined" in any query response
Nodes SHOULD respect quarantine notices but MAY choose not to, preserving the protocol's immutability guarantees.

section.t: Witness Ring Validation: Quarantine requests SHOULD be validated by the witness ring (5 of 7 witnesses) before being applied. The validation policy (e.g., evidence requirements, reason codes) is application- defined. The ring_signature in a QuarantineNotice MUST be a valid RingSignature as defined in .
Quarantine Removal: A quarantine MAY be removed by:

ul.li: Expiration of valid_until
A signed unquarantine request from the original requestor or owner
A witness ring resolution (if the quarantine was applied in error)

figure.artwork: UnquarantineRequest = [ "quip-v1", "unquarantine", trusted_cid: CIDOrV1, affected_cids: [* CIDOrV1], reason: tstr, timestamp: uint, requestor: NodeId, signature: bytes .size 64 ]

section.name: Derivative Linking
section.t: Applications MAY link derivative CIDs to Trusted CIDs. The mechanism for detecting derivatives (e.g., perceptual hashing, manual reporting) is application- defined.

figure.artwork: DerivativeLink = [ "quip-v1", "derivative_link", trusted_cid: CIDOrV1, derivative_cid: CIDOrV1, app_data: { * tstr => any }, ; Application-defined evidence link_type: tstr, ; "perceptual_hash", "manual", etc. timestamp: uint, reporter: NodeId, signature: bytes .size 64 ]

section.t: Derivative links MAY be used by applications to:

ul.li: Apply quarantine to all derivatives of a work
Implement "right to be forgotten" for all copies
Provide attribution across derivative works

section.name: Limitations and Caveats
section.t: The governance primitives have inherent limitations:

ul.li: No physical deletion: Quarantine is a discovery mechanism, not a deletion mechanism. Nodes MAY retain content but MUST honor quarantine for discovery queries.
Application-dependent: The effectiveness of governance depends on application policies (evidence requirements, perceptual hash algorithms, etc.).
Evasion possible: Content can be modified to evade detection. Applications SHOULD use multiple detection mechanisms.
Private networks: Content on private QUIP networks may not be visible to the public DHT and thus cannot be discovered or quarantined by public governance applications.

section.name: Application Examples (Non-Normative)
section.t: This section provides examples of how applications might use the governance primitives. These are illustrative and not protocol requirements.

ul.li: Application defines perceptual hash algorithms (pHash, dHash, etc.) in app_metadata
Application runs detection service that finds derivatives
Application submits derivative_link for each derivative
Application submits quarantine with all derivative CIDs
Witness ring validates based on application-defined evidence
Copyright holder registers tCID with ownership claim
Copyright holder delegates to DMCA agent
DMCA agent submits quarantine with evidence (court order, notice)
Witness ring validates the evidence
Network quarantines the content
User registers tCID for their personal data
User submits quarantine with reason="RtBF"
Witness ring validates the request
Network quarantines all derivatives linked to the tCID

section.name: Content Identifiers (CIDs)
section.t: A CID is a cryptographic hash that uniquely identifies content. QUIP supports multiple hash algorithms for CID generation:

tr.td: 3× faster, parallelizable, built-in keyed hashing, tree-based structure for partial verification

section.t: Both algorithms produce 32-byte digests, enabling consistent CID handling. The hash algorithm MUST be indicated in the handshake extensions during capability negotiation ().

CID Verification: Receivers MUST verify that the hash of the received payload matches the CID using the algorithm indicated in the handshake. For CIDv1, the algorithm is indicated in the CID itself. Mismatches MUST be rejected with E_CID_MISMATCH (error code 0x0C).
Algorithm Negotiation: Peers SHOULD negotiate the hash algorithm during the handshake. If no agreement is reached, the peers MUST fall back to SHA-256.

ul.li: Performance: BLAKE3 is approximately 3× faster than SHA-256 for large data, making it ideal for content-addressed storage.
Parallelization: BLAKE3's tree-based construction enables parallel hashing across multiple CPU cores.
Partial Verification: The Merkle tree structure enables verification of a single chunk without downloading the entire file. See .
Key Derivation: Built-in derive_key function supports key derivation and keyed hashing without a separate HMAC layer.

section.t: Why SHA-256 is Mandatory: SHA-256 ensures broad compatibility with existing systems and meets regulatory requirements for FIPS-compliant environments. BLAKE3 is provided as an OPTIONAL optimization for performance-critical applications.

section.name: CIDv1: Tagged Content Identifiers
section.t: To eliminate ambiguity across connections, QUIP supports an OPTIONAL tagged CID format, CIDv1, that includes the hash algorithm as a prefix. This ensures the same content yields the same CID regardless of the connection's negotiated hash algorithm.
Tagging: A CIDv1 is encoded as a CBOR map or as a binary prefix followed by the digest. The RECOMMENDED binary format is a single byte prefix (hash_algo) followed by the 32-byte digest:

figure.artwork: cidv1_bytes = [hash_algo: uint8] + [digest: 32-byte hash]

section.t: Usage: When both peers support CIDv1 (bit 9 set in capabilities), they MUST use CIDv1 for all persistent state — including pins, quarantine notices, trusted CID registrations, and derivative links. Raw CIDs MAY still be used for transient messages (e.g., RBSR range hashes) but SHOULD be migrated to CIDv1 on future interactions.
This ensures that:

ul.li: Pins and governance state are consistent across connections
Quarantine and derivative linking work across different hash algorithm preferences
DVV state CIDs are unambiguous

section.t: Negotiation: The cidv1_algo handshake extension indicates the preferred algorithm for CIDv1. If both peers support CIDv1, they MUST use the tagged format for all content identifiers. If no agreement is reached, peers MUST fall back to raw CIDs with the algorithm indicated by hash_algo.
Migration: Implementations that support CIDv1 SHOULD continue to accept raw CIDs for backward compatibility but MUST prefer CIDv1 for new persistent state.
Future Work: Full CIDv1 with multicodec prefix (IPFS-compatible) is deferred to .

section.name: Merkle Range Fetching (OPTIONAL)
section.t: BLAKE3's tree structure enables cryptographic verification of an arbitrary byte range within a resource without downloading the entire resource. QUIP exposes this capability through the merkle_range capability bit and the fetch_range / range_response verb pair. This mechanism is OPTIONAL and is only available when both peers advertise merkle_range and blake3.

Requirement: Range fetching is only defined for resources whose CID is a BLAKE3 CID (either a raw CID produced with hash_algo = 1 or a CIDv1 with hash_algo = 1). SHA-256 CIDs do not support range fetching because SHA-256 has no tree structure to prove against. Implementations MUST NOT advertise merkle_range without also advertising blake3; see the capability dependencies in .

Chunk Structure: BLAKE3 divides the input into chunks of BLAKE3_CHUNK_SIZE (1024 bytes). The tree of chunk chaining values is defined in the BLAKE3 specification . QUIP does not redefine this structure; it uses BLAKE3's native tree as the source of both the CID and the range proofs.

Range Request: A range request specifies a resource, a BLAKE3 CID, a byte offset, and a byte length. The responder returns the requested bytes and a proof that those bytes belong to the subtree whose chaining values fold up to the CID. The proof format is BLAKE3's verified streaming format, defined in the BLAKE3 specification. QUIP treats the proof as an opaque byte string whose interpretation is defined by BLAKE3.

Verification: The client receives the range bytes and the proof, and verifies them against the CID using BLAKE3's verification procedure. If verification fails, the client MUST reject the response with E_PROOF_INVALID (error code 0x1C).

Range Bounds: The range [offset, offset + length) MUST fall entirely within the resource. Requests whose range extends past the end of the resource MUST be rejected with E_RANGE_INVALID (error code 0x1B). Requests whose length exceeds MAX_RANGE_LENGTH (or the peer's advertised max_range_length) MUST be rejected with E_RANGE_INVALID.

Range Length Cap: To bound the memory cost of a single response, a range request MUST NOT exceed MAX_RANGE_LENGTH (1048576 bytes, 1 MiB) unless both peers negotiated a larger max_range_length via the handshake extension (0x0C). Peers that need to transfer more than the cap SHOULD issue multiple range requests in parallel, each covering a distinct range.

Responder Without a Cached Chunk Tree: A responder that advertises merkle_range is not required to keep the chunk tree resident for every resource it holds. If a fetch_range request arrives for a resource whose chunk tree is not cached, the responder MUST either (a) recompute the chunk tree from the blob on demand and serve the range, or (b) reject the request with E_RANGE_INVALID (error code 0x1B). A responder that chooses to recompute on demand SHOULD rate-limit such requests to bound the CPU cost, since recomputation is O(resource_size) and can be exploited for amplification. A responder SHOULD cache the chunk tree alongside the blob when the resource is written with merkle_range enabled, so that subsequent requests are O(log(resource_size)). The choice between recomputation and rejection is a local policy decision; the protocol does not mandate either behavior.

Rate Limiting: Range requests are subject to the same per-NodeId rate limits as other SYNC verbs. Implementations SHOULD additionally cap the total bytes served per connection per unit time to bound the cost of a peer issuing many small range requests.

Interaction with Other Verbs: Range fetching is additive. It does not modify the behavior of get, set, sync, rbsr_sync, or the BULK verbs. A resource whose entire content is needed SHOULD be fetched via the normal whole-resource mechanisms; range fetching is for partial reads.
Use Cases: Merkle range fetching is applicable whenever the content format exposes stable structure that a consumer can address by offset:

ul.li: Progressive MP4 playback, where the moov atom is fetched first and media fragments are fetched on demand.
PDF page navigation, where each page's byte range is fetched individually.
Large ISO images, where individual file entries are fetched by their offset in the ISO9660 directory.
BLAKE3-addressed VM disk images, where block-level chunks are fetched independently.
HTTP-style byte-range requests against any immutable BLAKE3-addressed resource.

section.t: For segmented formats that already expose independent sub-resources (HLS, DASH, fragmented MP4), range fetching is not required — the segments are already separately addressable. Range fetching is the mechanism for formats whose structure is only expressible as byte offsets into a single blob.

section.name: Threshold Signatures
section.t: To defend against endpoint compromise, QUIP supports threshold signatures using the FROST scheme .

figure.artwork: ThresholdSignature = { "scheme": "FROST-ED25519-v1", "participants": [* NodeId], "threshold": uint, ; t (e.g., 2) "signature": bytes, ; Aggregate signature "commitments": [* bytes] }

section.t: Threshold signatures are OPTIONAL. Users MAY choose single-device keys for simplicity. The FROST group public key serves as the NodeId. The aggregated threshold signature is verified using standard Ed25519 verification; witnesses need no FROST-specific logic. Key rotation requires t-of-n participants to sign the rotation message.

Ring Signature Compatibility: The FROST aggregate signature format in FrostRingSig () uses the same FROST scheme. Witnesses implementing checkpointing SHOULD support both individual and FROST aggregate signatures for maximum interoperability.

section.name: QUIP-CBOR
section.t: QUIP-CBOR is with the following additional constraints:

ul.li: Integers: Shortest form only.
Maps: Keys sorted by bytewise lexicographic order.
Floats: Prohibited. Use integer + scale.
Tags: No CBOR tags are used for QUIP messages. All messages begin with the string "quip-v1" as the first array element.
Indefinite lengths: Prohibited.

section.t: Non-canonical CBOR MUST be rejected with error E_BAD_ENCODING.

Version Gate: Implementations that dispatch on element 1 of the top-level array MUST treat element 0 as a version gate: if element 0 is not the string "quip-v1", the message MUST be rejected with E_BAD_ENCODING (for unknown version) before any verb-specific parsing occurs.

section.name: Signing Convention
section.t: Every QUIP message that carries a signature field uses the same signing convention. This convention is normative and applies to all signed messages in this specification, including but not limited to: KeyClaim, WitnessStatement, KeyRotation, Discontinuity, SeqReset, RevocationNotice, TrustedCIDRegistration, DelegationCertificate, QuarantineRequest, UnquarantineRequest, DerivativeLink, ConnectivityAnnounce, CandidateAnnounce, RelayDiscovery, RelayResponse, CoralLookup, SpilloverRequest, SpilloverResponse, CrossPathValidation, CrossPathResult, and all BFT message types.
The signing payload is defined as follows:

ol.li: Remove the signature element entirely from the message array. The element is omitted, not zeroed, not replaced with null, and not truncated in place. If the signature field is named signature, owner_sig, witness_sig, primary_sig, or ring_signature, that entire field is removed.
Re-encode the remaining array using the canonical QUIP-CBOR rules of this section. The result is the signing_payload.
Compute the signature over signing_payload using Ed25519 . The signature is the raw 64-byte Ed25519 signature.

section.t: Signature Algorithm: Ed25519 . No other signature algorithm is defined for version 1 of this protocol.

ol.li: Extract the signature element from the received message.
Re-encode the message array without that element using QUIP-CBOR (canonical form as defined in ).

li.t: Verify the Ed25519 signature against the signer's public key:

ul.li: For self-signed messages (e.g., KeyClaim, SeqReset), the signer's public key is the NodeId field of the message.
For messages signed by a node other than their subject (e.g., WitnessStatement signed by the witness), the signer's public key is the NodeId of the signing party as identified by the message.
For ring signatures, see the rules below.

ol.li: Reject the message with E_VIOLATION (error code 0x07) if verification fails.

section.t: Ring Signature Signing: For messages containing a ring_signature field (e.g., QuarantineNotice, bft_state_transfer), all signatures within the ring signature cover the same signing payload:

ul.li: IndividualRingSig: Each signature in signatures[i] is computed by signers[i] over the same signing_payload (the enclosing message with the ring_signature element removed). The signer list signers and the signature list signatures MUST have the same length and MUST be ordered by canonical NodeId order (bytewise lexicographic). The ring_signature element is removed as a whole before encoding — the individual signatures inside it are not separately excluded.

FrostRingSig: The FROST aggregate signature is computed by the FROST group over the same signing_payload (the enclosing message with the ring_signature element removed). The FROST verification procedure of is applied against the group public key.

section.t: Nested Signatures: If a signed message contains another signed message as an embedded value (for example, a CrossPathValidation message embedding one or more signed LookupResponse values in its path_responses field), the outer signature covers the inner message as encoded on the wire, including any nested signature fields. Nested messages are not stripped during the encoding of the outer signing_payload. Implementations MUST preserve the encoded bytes of any nested signed message when computing the outer signing payload.

Multiple Signatures on the Same Message: Messages that require multiple independent signatures (e.g., a message co-signed by two NodeIds) are represented as separate fields, not as a single field of multiple signatures. Each such field is removed independently for its own signing payload. Implementations MUST NOT interpret the removal of one signature field as also removing another.

Determinism Requirement: Because the signing payload is derived by removing an element and re-encoding, implementations MUST use QUIP-CBOR canonical encoding (as defined in ) at every step. In particular, integers MUST use the shortest form, map keys MUST be sorted, and no CBOR tags or indefinite-length items may appear. Non-canonical encodings would cause the re-encoded payload to differ from the signer's intent and cause verification failure.

Test Vectors: Implementers SHOULD use the test vectors published at the URL given in to validate their signing and verification implementation. The test vectors cover at least: one self-signed message (KeyClaim), one witness-signed message (WitnessStatement), one IndividualRingSig, and one FrostRingSig.

section.name: Transport Tiers
section.t: QUIP uses four dedicated transport tiers to eliminate head-of-line blocking and ensure deterministic behavior.

figure.artwork:
QUIP Message (as placed on a reliable stream): +------------------+----------------------------------+ | varint | QUIP-CBOR object | | length (1-8 B) | ["quip-v1", ...] | +------------------+----------------------------------+
Note: QUIP messages begin with the string "quip-v1" as the first array element. No CBOR tag is used for QUIP messages.
QUIC Control Stream (T0, stream 0): +------------------+----------------+----------------+ | QUIP Handshake | QUIP Message 1 | QUIP Message 2 | +------------------+----------------+----------------+
QUIC DATAGRAM (T3, RFC 9221 — no framing needed, one QUIP-CBOR object per datagram): +---------------------------------------------------+ | ["quip-v1", "emit", event_type, payload] | +---------------------------------------------------+

tr.td: Handshake, errors, KT witness, key_claim, pin_announce, resource_announce, governance operations, BFT messages, connectivity_announce, candidate_announce, spillover operations, coral cluster management
DVV exchange, anti-entropy, state reconciliation, RBSR sync, Merkle range fetching (fetch_range / range_response)
Messages, documents, reliable data transfer, CID payloads
Media, telemetry, presence, ephemeral events, pin gossip

section.t: These stream IDs are reserved QUIC stream IDs. Implementations MUST NOT use these IDs for non-QUIP traffic.

ul.li: BLOCK(0x01): Receiver cannot accept more data
UNBLOCK(0x02): Receiver is ready to accept data
WINDOW(0x03): Receiver advertises available capacity in bytes

section.name: NAT Traversal and Connectivity Establishment
section.t: QUIC, as a connection-oriented protocol, requires a direct 5-tuple (source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port, protocol) between endpoints. However, in many deployment scenarios, peers are behind Network Address Translators (NATs) that prevent direct inbound connections. This section describes the NAT traversal mechanisms used by QUIP.

Core Principle: QUIP does not rely on centralized NAT traversal servers. Instead, NAT traversal is performed using the Coral DHT for address discovery, hole punching coordination, and relay selection, ensuring the protocol remains brokerless and decentralized.

section.name: Coral DHT-Assisted NAT Traversal
section.t: QUIP uses the Coral DHT for NAT traversal in three ways:

ul.li: Address Discovery: Peers publish their external addresses to the DHT
Hole Punching: Peers coordinate connectivity establishment via the DHT
Relay Discovery: Peers discover relay nodes through the DHT

section.t: Address Type: All NAT traversal messages share a single Address type, defined once here and used throughout this section:
Connectivity Announcement: Each peer publishes its connectivity information to the Coral DHT:

figure.artwork: ConnectivityAnnounce = [ "quip-v1", "connectivity_announce", node_id: NodeId, external_addr: Address, ; DHT-observed external address internal_addr: Address, ; Internal address (if known) nat_type: uint, ; See "NAT Type Values" below. port_preservation: bool, ; Whether NAT preserves source port relay_capable: bool, ; Can relay for others capacity: uint, ; Relay capacity (if relay_capable) timestamp: uint, ; Unix milliseconds signature: bytes .size 64 ; Signed by node_id ]

tr.td: NAT type not yet determined; external address observations are insufficient to classify it.
Directly reachable; no NAT in the path. The observed external address equals the internal address.

Full-cone or restricted-cone NAT. The external IP is stable across destinations; the external port is stable across destinations (full-cone) or stable once a destination has been contacted (restricted-cone).
Port-restricted cone. The external IP is stable but the external port varies with the destination's IP.
External IP or port varies per destination. Direct connectivity is not achievable and a relay is required. See .

section.t: DHT-Assisted Address Discovery: Implementations SHOULD use the Coral DHT to request address discovery from other peers. A peer MAY ask multiple independent DHT peers to report the source Address observed for its request and use the most consistent result as external_addr. Implementations MUST NOT depend on STUN or any centralized address-discovery service.

Connectivity TTL: Connectivity announcements have a TTL of CONNECTIVITY_TTL (600 seconds, 10 minutes). Peers SHOULD re-announce every 480 seconds (8 minutes) to maintain freshness. This longer TTL reduces DHT traffic while maintaining timely connectivity information.

Adaptive Re-announce: Peers MAY adjust re-announce frequency based on observed churn rate. In stable networks, peers MAY extend re-announce intervals up to 90% of TTL. In high-churn networks, peers SHOULD reduce intervals to 50% of TTL.

section.name: Coral DHT Relay System
section.t: The Coral DHT provides a decentralized relay system for peers behind NATs that cannot establish direct connections.
Relay Discovery: Peers discover relays by querying the Coral DHT for nodes that advertise relay capability:

Request/response correlation: A requester may have multiple relay_discovery requests outstanding for different targets. To allow a driver to demultiplex responses without serializing discoveries per target:

ul.li: The request_id in a RelayDiscovery MUST be a freshly generated 16-byte value, unique among the requester's outstanding discoveries. Implementations SHOULD generate it from a cryptographically secure random source.
A RelayResponse MUST echo both request_id and target from the RelayDiscovery it answers.
A requester that receives a RelayResponse whose request_id does not match any outstanding discovery MUST discard the response.

A requester that receives a RelayResponse whose target does not match the target of the matching outstanding discovery MUST discard the response; a mismatch is evidence of a response-spoofing attempt and SHOULD be logged.

section.t: This removes the earlier constraint that a requester serialize discoveries per target, and allows a single driver to have multiple in-flight discoveries while still demultiplexing responses unambiguously.
Relay Selection Algorithm: Peers select relays using the following criteria:

ol.li: XOR distance to target (Kademlia-style)
Available capacity (capacity - load)
Cost metric (lower is better)
Geographic proximity (if available from cluster info)
Historical reliability (prefer relays with good uptime)

section.t: Relay Selection Attack Mitigations: An attacker could operate relays that refuse to forward traffic or selectively drop packets. To mitigate this:

ul.li: Multiple relays: Peers SHOULD use at least 2 relays for critical operations; traffic is sent through both, and the first response is accepted
Relay verification: Peers SHOULD verify relay functionality before sending sensitive traffic by sending a test packet and waiting for acknowledgment
Relay reputation: Peers SHOULD maintain a reputation score for relays based on successful vs. failed relays; relays with poor reputation are avoided
Relay chaining fallback: If a relay fails, the peer SHOULD immediately fall back to an alternative relay
Relay failure monitoring: Peers SHOULD monitor relay failure patterns; coordinated failures from a cluster of relays may indicate an attack

section.t: Relay Chaining: When direct connectivity is impossible, peers MAY chain multiple relays (up to RELAY_HOP_LIMIT):

ul.li: KEM: DHKEM(X25519, HKDF-SHA256)
KDF: HKDF-SHA256
AEAD: ChaCha20Poly1305

section.t: The recipient public key is the X25519 public key derived from relay_id via the standard Ed25519-to-X25519 birational map (, Section 4.1.2; as implemented by crypto_sign_ed25519_pk_to_curve25519 in libsodium and by age). The HPKE info string is the UTF-8 encoding of "QUIP-relay-hop-v1"; the aad is empty.

Plaintext layout: The plaintext is the symmetric traffic key that the relay uses to decrypt the relayed payload for this hop, followed by the trailing portion of the relay chain beyond this hop (encoded as a QUIP-CBOR RelayChain). The exact layout of the symmetric traffic key is defined by the relay transport profile and is not part of this specification; the requirement this specification places on encrypted_key is only that it is a well-formed HPKE seal under the recipient's derived X25519 key with the suite above and the plaintext layout just described.

Chain order: The hops array in RelayChain is ordered from the sender outward: hops[0] is the first relay the sender sends to, hops[n-1] is the last relay before the target. Each RelayHop.relay_id names the relay that receives that hop and decrypts encrypted_key; next_hop is the address of the following relay (or, for the last hop, the address of the target).

Because encrypted_key now has a defined scheme, multi-hop relay chains are fully wire-format-defined: an implementation that can perform the birational map and HPKE with the suite above can interoperate with any other implementation that follows this section.

Base-mode rationale: HPKE mode_base (no sender authentication inside HPKE) is used deliberately. The relay chain as a whole is signed by its sender (see ); per-hop sender authentication would be redundant and would enlarge the ciphertext. Recipients of a relay chain verify the sender's signature at the chain level, not per hop.

Relay Chaining Performance: Relay chains of RELAY_HOP_LIMIT (2) hops add approximately 100-300ms of latency per hop. For latency-sensitive operations (T3 datagrams, real-time media), implementations SHOULD use direct connections when possible and MAY bypass relays for high-priority traffic if direct connectivity is available.

Relay Capacity Management: Relays SHOULD limit their capacity to prevent DoS. The RECOMMENDED capacity is RELAY_CAPACITY (1000) concurrent relay connections. Relays SHOULD evict least-recently-used connections when capacity is exceeded.

Relay Security Model: Relays are selected from the Coral DHT using the same XOR distance metric and multiple paths. A malicious relay cannot corrupt traffic as all communication is QUIC+TLS 1.3 encrypted. However, a relay could refuse to forward traffic or perform DoS attacks. Implementations SHOULD:

ul.li: Use multiple relays for critical operations
Monitor for relay failure patterns
Rotate relays periodically
Rate-limit relay connections per NodeId

section.t: Relay Sybil Protection: The same XOR distance metric that protects witness rings protects relay selection. An attacker must control XOR-close relay nodes to influence selection, which is computationally infeasible. Additionally, the 3-path lookup ensures relay selection diversity.

section.name: Candidate Exchange
section.t: QUIP uses an ICE-like mechanism for candidate gathering and prioritization, but with the Coral DHT replacing the signaling server:

figure.artwork:
CandidateAnnounce = [ "quip-v1", "candidate_announce", node_id: NodeId, candidates: [* Candidate], session_id: bytes .size 16, ; Unique session identifier timestamp: uint, signature: bytes .size 64 ]
Candidate = { addr: Address, type: uint, ; 0 = host, 1 = server-reflexive ; (DHT-observed external address), ; 2 = relayed, 3 = peer-reflexive priority: uint, foundation: tstr, component: uint }

section.t: Candidate Gathering: Peers gather candidates from:

ul.li: Host candidates: Local network interfaces
Server-reflexive candidates: Via the Coral DHT (peers request address discovery from DHT nodes)
Relayed candidates: Via Coral DHT relays
Peer-reflexive candidates: Via connectivity checks

section.t: Candidate Prioritization: Candidates SHOULD be prioritized using the following scheme (highest to lowest):

ul.li: Host candidates: Highest priority (direct connection)
Server-reflexive candidates: Second priority (DHT-observed)
Peer-reflexive candidates: Third priority (discovered during connectivity checks)
Relayed candidates: Lowest priority (highest latency, least reliable)

section.t: This ensures that direct connections are preferred over relays, and that lower-latency candidates are tried before higher-latency alternatives. Implementations MAY adjust priorities based on observed performance.
Connectivity Checks: Peers perform connectivity checks using QUIC's path validation mechanism:

ol.li: Peer A publishes candidates to the DHT for session S
Peer B retrieves A's candidates
B sends a QUIC path validation packet to A's candidates
A responds to valid paths
Both peers record reachable paths

section.t: Path Validation Without an Endpoint: The mechanism above describes the check at the protocol level. At the transport level, a QUIP driver that does not own a QUIC Endpoint cannot perform QUIC path validation directly. The RECOMMENDED approach is for the application that owns the Endpoint to perform the check on the driver's behalf:

ol.li: The driver signals the application that a probe is needed, passing the candidate address and the session identifier.

The application opens a short-lived QUIC connection to the candidate address with the same ALPN as the main connection. The connection establishment itself is the reachability check; the probe is not a migration of the main connection and does not validate a path on it. Where the application's QUIC stack exposes the path validation procedure of , Section 8.2, the application MAY use it as an additional liveness signal.
The application reports success or failure back to the driver, together with the session identifier so the result can be matched to the outstanding probe.
The application closes the probe connection regardless of outcome. Probe connections are not retained and are not reused for application traffic.

section.t: A probe connection MUST use a fresh QUIC connection, not an existing one. The client certificate on a probe connection MUST NOT be assumed to authenticate either party: the probe's purpose is to establish reachability, not identity. A candidate that succeeds is recorded by the driver in the session's candidate table; a candidate that fails is marked so the driver does not re-probe it during the same session. Implementations SHOULD cap the number of concurrent probe connections per session (RECOMMENDED: 3) and SHOULD apply the 5-second connectivity-check timeout recommended in .
Candidate Security: An attacker could inject false candidates to cause connection attempts to malicious endpoints. To prevent this:

ul.li: Signature verification: All CandidateAnnounce messages are signed by the NodeId; recipients MUST verify the signature before accepting candidates
Candidate validation: Recipients SHOULD validate candidates by sending a connectivity check before using them for sensitive traffic
Anti-spoofing: Candidates that fail connectivity checks are discarded; repeated failures from the same source trigger rate limiting
Candidate pruning: Candidates are automatically pruned after CANDIDATE_TTL (RECOMMENDED: 30 seconds) if not verified
Session binding: Candidates are bound to the session_id; candidates from different sessions are rejected

figure.artwork: CANDIDATE_TTL = 30 ; seconds

section.name: Coral DHT Integration
section.t: QUIP uses a Coral DHT for resilient witness discovery, NAT traversal, and resource discovery. QUIP-Coral is based on the Coral DHT design with the following adaptations for federation and identity. Coral's two principal goals—avoiding hot spots and finding nearby data without querying distant nodes—align directly with QUIP's requirements for witness ring discovery and decentralized persistence.

Coral DHT Structure: The Coral DHT organizes peers into hierarchical clusters based on network proximity. Each peer belongs to one cluster at each level. The current implementation uses a three-level hierarchy consistent with the Coral design :

tr.td: Fast witness discovery for nearby peers

section.t: Each cluster is named by an m-bit cluster identifier (cid); the global cid0 is predefined as 0m. Nodes maintain the same NodeId in all clusters to which they belong, enabling seamless lookup continuation across levels. For a discussion of why these thresholds were chosen, see .
Constants: The following constants apply to Coral DHT operation:

tr.td: Maximum split attempts before creating new cluster
Number of gateway routers to use for discovery

section.name: Distributed Sloppy Hash Table
section.t: Coral introduces the Distributed Sloppy Hash Table (DSHT) abstraction , which is specifically suited to locating replicated resources. DSHTs sacrifice the consistency of DHTs to support both frequent fetches and frequent stores of the same hash table key. The fundamental observation is that a node does not need to know every replicated location of a resource—it only needs a single, valid, nearby copy.

ul.li: put(key, value): Stores a value under a key. A key may have multiple values.
get(key): Returns some subset of the values stored under a key.

section.t: Sloppy Storage: Each node stores only some maximum number of values for a particular key. When the number of values exceeds this maximum, they are spread across multiple nodes via "spillover." When a node's list under a key is full, the inserting node backtracks one hop on the lookup path and appends the value there. This eliminates hot spots—multiple stores on the same key will not overload any one node.
In QUIP, DSHT is used for:

ul.li: Storing witness announcements (witness_announce) under the target NodeId
Storing resource location hints (resource_announce) under the resource_id
Storing connectivity announcements (connectivity_announce) under the NodeId
Storing cluster membership information for self-organization

section.name: Cluster Acceptance
section.t: A node MUST only join a cluster if it is acceptable, meaning that the latency to at least CLUSTER_ACCEPTANCE_PERCENTILE (90%) of nodes in the cluster is below the cluster's RTT threshold. This property is easy for a node to test by collecting round-trip times to a subset of nodes in the cluster, perhaps by simply looking up its own identifier as part of joining.
Acceptance Testing: To determine if a cluster is acceptable, a node SHOULD:

ol.li: Obtain a random subset of at least 20 nodes from the cluster
Measure round-trip time (RTT) to each node using QUIC ping
Sort measured RTTs
If the 90th percentile RTT is ≤ the cluster threshold, the cluster is acceptable

section.t: Rejection: If a cluster is not acceptable, the node MUST NOT join it and MUST attempt to find a lower-level cluster or create a new one. A node unable to find an acceptable cluster creates a new one with a random cid.

section.name: Cluster Discovery
section.t: New nodes discover clusters using network topology hints and the DSHT interface.
Gateway Router Discovery: Upon joining the network, a node SHOULD:

ol.li: Perform a traceroute to a known bootstrap node
Extract the first GATEWAY_ROUTER_COUNT (5) gateway router IP addresses
For each gateway router IP ip, perform put(hash(ip), nodeaddr) in the global cluster (level 0)

section.t: Cluster Lookup: A new node looking for a nearby cluster SHOULD:

ol.li: Perform traceroute to a bootstrap node
Extract gateway router IPs
For each IP, perform get(hash(ip)) in the global cluster
Collect node addresses from responses
Test these nodes for cluster acceptability using the procedure in

section.t: Fallback: If no acceptable cluster is found via gateway routers, the node MUST use the configured bootstrap nodes to join the global cluster and discover clusters through normal DHT lookups.

section.name: Cluster Merging
section.t: When a node knows of two acceptable clusters at the same level, it will join the larger one. If a node switches clusters, it still remains in the routing tables of nodes in its old cluster. Old neighbors will still contact it; the node replies to level-i requests originating outside its current cluster with:
This produces an avalanche effect as more and more nodes switch to the larger cluster.

Preference Function (δ): To prevent oscillations between similarly sized clusters, nodes MUST use a preference function δ that shifts every MERGE_DELTA_INTERVAL (1 hour). A node selects the larger cluster only if:

figure.artwork: |log(sizeA) - log(sizeB)| > δ(min(ageA, ageB))

section.t: where sizeA and sizeB are the estimated cluster sizes, ageA and ageB are the cluster creation times, and δ is defined as:

figure.artwork: δ(t) = 0 if floor(t / MERGE_DELTA_INTERVAL) is even δ(t) = 2 if floor(t / MERGE_DELTA_INTERVAL) is odd

ul.li: If |log(sizeA) - log(sizeB)| > δ, the node MUST join the larger cluster
If |log(sizeA) - log(sizeB)| ≤ δ, the node MUST join the cluster with the lower cluster_id (deterministic tie-breaking)

section.t: Stability Guarantee: This preference function ensures that clusters of disproportionate size merge immediately, while similarly sized clusters eventually converge to a stable state when δ = 2 forces flow to the lower cluster_id.

section.name: Cluster Splitting
section.t: If a cluster's 90th percentile RTT exceeds its threshold for more than CLUSTER_HEARTBEAT * 3 (3 minutes), the cluster SHOULD split.

Split Center: Each cluster defines a center c as the node closest to hash(cluster_id) in the DSHT. Define cidN = hash(cid) and cidF as cidN with the high-order bit flipped. The cluster center c is the node closest to key cidN in the DSHT.
Split Algorithm: When a node detects that its cluster needs to split:

ol.li: The node performs a get on hash(cidN)
If the get returns the center c, the node measures RTT to c
If the RTT to c is ≤ the cluster threshold, the node joins the "near" cluster (cidN)
If the RTT to c is > the cluster threshold, the node attempts to join the "far" cluster (cidF)
If neither cluster is acceptable, the node creates a new cluster with a random cluster_id

section.t: Sloppy Replication for Splits: To avoid overloading the center c, nodes MAY use sloppy replication:

ul.li: Nodes that have already split SHOULD perform put(cidN, nodeaddr) in the old cluster
New nodes perform get(cidN) and learn a random subset of split nodes
Nodes that find cidN acceptable join it without pinging the center

section.t: Split Limit: If a node fails to find an acceptable cluster after MAX_SPLIT_ATTEMPTS (RECOMMENDED: 3), it MUST create a new cluster with a random cluster_id. Except in the case of pathological network topologies, a small number of splits should suffice to reach a stable state.

section.name: Cluster Size Estimation
section.t: Nodes MUST maintain an estimate of their cluster size for merging decisions. The expected O(log n) number of routing RPCs provides a rough estimate of total network size.
Size Estimation Method: Nodes estimate cluster size using the routing table size of the underlying lookup protocol:

figure.artwork: size = 2^(average_routing_table_size)

section.t: where average_routing_table_size is the average number of nodes in the routing table entries at each distance level.
Size Propagation: When a node switches clusters, it MUST reply to requests from its old cluster with the cluster information tuple defined in .
Size Validation: Nodes SHOULD cross-validate cluster size estimates from multiple sources before using them for merging decisions.

section.name: Multiple Lookup Paths
section.t: QUIP extends the Coral design with multiple independent lookup paths for each key, preventing path-based attacks. This is not present in the original Coral paper but is a critical security enhancement for QUIP's witness discovery.

figure.artwork:
CoralLookup = [ "quip-v1", "coral_lookup", key: bytes .size 32, lookup_paths: [* LookupPath], witness_ring_id: bytes .size 32, timestamp: uint, requester: NodeId, signature: bytes .size 64 ]
LookupPath = { path_id: bytes .size 16, nodes: [* NodeId], ; Path through DHT nodes value_hash: bytes .size 32, ; Hash of expected value ttl: uint ; Time-to-live in seconds }

section.t: Independent Paths: QUIP provides at least LOOKUP_PATHS (3) independent lookup paths per key. Each path uses different DHT nodes, preventing:

ul.li: Path-based witness rejection: An attacker cannot reject a witness by controlling a single path
Eclipse attacks: Multiple paths prevent isolation
Sybil attacks: Coral's redundancy makes Sybil attacks more expensive

section.t: Path Verification: Lookup responses include cryptographic proof that each path was followed correctly:

figure.artwork:
LookupResponse = [ "quip-v1", "coral_lookup_response", key: bytes .size 32, values: [* bytes], path_proofs: [* PathProof], responder: NodeId, timestamp: uint, signature: bytes .size 64 ]
PathProof = { path_id: bytes .size 16, node_signatures: [* bytes .size 64], value_hash: bytes .size 32, responded: bool }

section.t: Path Independence: The 3 lookup paths MUST be independent. Two paths are independent if they share no nodes and originate from different clusters. If path independence cannot be verified, the peer MUST raise the consensus threshold to 3-of-3.

section.name: Attack Circumvention
section.t: QUIP extends Coral's sloppy replication and multiple-cluster design with explicit attack circumvention mechanisms. These are not present in the original Coral paper but are critical for QUIP's security model.

section.name: Spillover Mechanism
section.t: When an attacker on the path falsely rejects a witness or prompts for spillover, QUIP provides a spillover mechanism that leverages Coral's sloppy replication and multiple lookup paths:

figure.artwork:
SpilloverRequest = [ "quip-v1", "spillover", original_key: bytes .size 32, rejected_witnesses: [* NodeId], rejection_reason: uint, ; 0 = timeout, 1 = invalid signature, ; 2 = conflicting claims, 3 = network error alternate_paths: [* LookupPath], requester: NodeId, timestamp: uint, signature: bytes .size 64 ]
SpilloverResponse = [ "quip-v1", "spillover_response", original_key: bytes .size 32, alternate_witnesses: [* NodeId], path_proofs: [* PathProof], consensus: uint, ; 0 = no consensus, 1 = partial, ; 2 = full consensus responder: NodeId, timestamp: uint, signature: bytes .size 64 ]

ul.li: Witness rejection without valid cryptographic proof
Inconsistent responses from witnesses on the same path
Timeout from all witnesses on a path (indicating path attack)
Conflicting witness claims that cannot be resolved
DHT node returns inconsistent DVV states

ol.li: Peer P detects a witness rejection or spillover prompt
P records the rejection and path information
P sends a SpilloverRequest to the Coral DHT
The DHT routes the request through independent paths (leveraging Coral's hierarchical clusters)
Each path performs its own witness discovery independently
P collects responses from all paths
P reaches consensus on the valid witness ring
If SPILLOVER_THRESHOLD (2) of LOOKUP_PATHS (3) paths agree, P accepts that witness ring
If no consensus is reached, P uses the most common set
If persistent disagreement, P escalates to fallback witnesses

section.t: Spillover Denial-of-Service Protection: An attacker could trigger spillover without succeeding in false witness rejection, causing performance degradation. To prevent this:

ul.li: Rate limiting: Spillover requests are rate-limited to 10 per minute per NodeId (see below)
Spillover cost: Each spillover request requires a small proof-of-work (RECOMMENDED: 2^20 hash iterations) to prevent automated triggering
Cached responses: Spillover responses are cached for SPILLOVER_CACHE_TTL (5 minutes); repeated requests for the same key return cached results
Reputation scoring: Nodes that repeatedly exceed the spillover rate limit have their requests de-prioritized
Exponential backoff: After 3 failed spillover attempts, the peer MUST wait 30 seconds before retrying

section.t: Spillover Rate Limiting: Spillover rate limiting MUST be enforced per NodeId across all connections. The RECOMMENDED limit is 10 spillover requests per minute per NodeId. A NodeId that exceeds the limit SHOULD be temporarily blacklisted for 5 minutes. The blacklisting MUST be applied consistently across all connected peers to prevent circumvention through connection switching.

section.name: Cross-Path Validation
section.t: To prevent attackers from controlling multiple paths, QUIP provides cross-path validation that leverages Coral's hierarchical clusters:

figure.artwork:
CrossPathValidation = [ "quip-v1", "cross_path_validation", key: bytes .size 32, path_responses: [* LookupResponse], witness_ring: [* NodeId], requester: NodeId, timestamp: uint, signature: bytes .size 64 ]

ul.li: Each path's witness ring must have MIN_WITNESSES (4+) witnesses
Witness rings from different paths must agree on at least DEGRADED_QUORUM (3) witnesses
If SPILLOVER_THRESHOLD (2) of LOOKUP_PATHS (3) paths agree, the consensus is accepted
If no consensus, the peer SHOULD wait and retry
Persistent disagreement triggers a network-wide alert

section.t: Cross-Path Collusion Detection: An attacker could control 2 of 3 paths by compromising nodes on multiple paths. To detect this:

ul.li: Path independence verification: QUIP ensures that paths use disjoint sets of nodes. Implementations SHOULD verify that no node appears on more than one path.
Path diversity checking: Peers SHOULD check that paths come from different network vantage points (different autonomous systems, different geographic regions).
Cross-path node comparison: If two paths return identical witness rings but use different nodes to discover them, this is a strong indicator of legitimacy.
Consensus threshold adjustment: If path independence cannot be verified (e.g., due to network constraints), the consensus threshold SHOULD be raised to 3-of-3, with fallback to cached witnesses.
Anomaly detection: If the same witnesses appear on all 3 paths but the paths use overlapping nodes, this may indicate an eclipse attack.

section.name: RTT Threshold Selection
section.t: The Coral paper presents measurements from the Gnutella network that inform the RTT thresholds. The cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) of measured RTTs between 12 RON nodes and approximately 2000 Gnutella peers showed smooth curves without distinct plateaus, giving relative freedom in setting cluster thresholds.

The choice of 30ms for level 2 covers smaller clusters of nodes, while the level 1 threshold of 100ms spans continents. For example, the expected RTT between New York and Berkeley is 68ms, and 72ms between Amsterdam and Athens. Low-level clusters are especially useful for sparse regions like Korea, where most queries of a traditional peer-to-peer system would go to North America.

QUIP adopts these thresholds based on the Coral measurements. Implementations MAY adjust these thresholds based on observed network conditions, but SHOULD maintain the three-level hierarchy to ensure compatibility with the Coral DHT design.

section.name: Comparison to Standard Coral CDN
section.t: QUIP's Coral DHT adapts the Coral CDN's clustering and redundancy principles for witness discovery and NAT traversal, rather than for content caching. The key innovations from Coral—sloppy storage, hierarchical clusters, self-organizing merge/split, and the DSHT abstraction—are applied to the DHT routing layer, not to content distribution.

This adaptation is appropriate because witness discovery requires the same properties as content discovery: resilience to attacks, geographic distribution, and fault tolerance. By applying Coral's principles to the routing layer, QUIP achieves these properties without requiring content caching infrastructure.

ul.li: Multiple lookup paths (3): Extends Coral's single-lookup design for path-based attack resilience
Spillover mechanism: Explicit attack circumvention when witnesses are falsely rejected
Cryptographic verification: All Coral operations in QUIP are signed and verified
Witness ring integration: Coral clusters serve witness discovery, not content caching

section.t: Nullable positional fields: In set, query_pins, and query_quarantined, a null in a positional slot means "this filter is absent" and is permitted only when a later positional slot in the same message is non-null. A null at the last occupied position is NOT RECOMMENDED — senders SHOULD omit the trailing field instead, and receivers SHOULD normalize a trailing null to absence. A null in a position that is not followed by any non-null field is redundant and carries no additional meaning.
The four logical query shapes and their canonical wire forms are:

tr.td: Filter by both resource_id and cid

ul.li: algo=0 (XOR): MUST be implemented. Simple XOR of range hashes. Fast but collision-prone for very large sets.
algo=1 (IBLT): MAY be implemented. Invertible Bloom Lookup Tables. Efficient for set differences but more complex.
algo=2 (Merkle): MAY be implemented. Merkle tree roots. Highest security but highest overhead.

section.t: Peers SHOULD negotiate the fingerprint algorithm via the rbsr_algo handshake extension (0x08). If no agreement is reached, the peer MUST fall back to XOR (algo=0).

Hash Algorithm in SET: The hash_algo field in the set verb indicates the algorithm used to generate the CID. If omitted, SHA-256 is assumed. For CIDv1, the algorithm is indicated in the CID itself and this field is ignored.

Nullable previous_cid: When a sender wishes to signal hash_algo without a previous_cid — for example, to declare the algorithm used for the current cid on a first write — it MUST encode the previous_cid slot as null and place the hash_algo value in the following position. Receivers MUST accept this form and treat the previous_cid as absent. The alternative — omitting previous_cid entirely and encoding hash_algo at the previous_cid position — is NOT RECOMMENDED, because it is indistinguishable from a future extension that might assign a non-uint meaning to that slot.

Merkle Range Fetching: The fetch_range verb is defined in . It requires the merkle_range capability bit and a BLAKE3 CID. Requests whose cid is not a BLAKE3 CID MUST be rejected with E_RANGE_INVALID (error code 0x1B). Responses whose proof fails verification MUST be rejected with E_PROOF_INVALID (error code 0x1C).

CausalOrder Is Not a Wire Type: Sync verbs carry DVV values, not CausalOrder classifications. The receiver re-derives the causal relationship from the DVVs as specified in . Implementations MUST NOT add a CausalOrder field to any sync message or any other message in this specification.

Pin Announcement: Peers SHOULD broadcast pin announcements via T3 to propagate pinning intent across the network. Implementations SHOULD limit pin announcements to 100 per minute per NodeId to prevent DoS.

This is distinct from a witness ring signature (5 of 7) used for consensus operations. Implementations SHOULD verify that the witness is a member of the current witness ring for the resource being announced.

section.name: Resource Discovery
section.t: QUIP provides a resource discovery mechanism to locate where a resource is hosted. The discovery mechanism is NAT-aware and uses the Coral DHT's multiple paths.

li.t: A peer announces a resource via resource_announce on T0. The announcement includes:

ul.li: resource_id — the name of the resource
latest_cid — the current CID (or CIDv1) of the resource
witness_ring — the witness ring for this resource
dht_locations — DHT node IDs that can serve the resource
relay_locations — Coral DHT relays that can serve the resource

li.t: A peer queries for a resource via query_resource on T0. The query includes:

ul.li: resource_id — the name to look up
OPTIONAL cid — a specific version (CID or CIDv1) to look up

li.t: The Coral DHT stores resource metadata with multiple replicas:

ul.li: resource_id → list of location hints
Location hints are NodeIds that can serve the content
Relay hints for NATed peers

ol.li: When a resource is updated, the peer SHOULD re-announce the resource with the new CID.

section.t: NAT-Aware Fetching: When fetching a resource:

ol.li: Peer P queries the Coral DHT for resource locations
P attempts direct QUIC connection to each location
If direct connection fails, P attempts via Coral relays
If relays fail, P requests spillover from DHT
P fetches from the first successful location
P verifies content integrity via CID

section.t: NAT-Hosted Resources: If the resource host is behind a NAT, the resource_announce MUST include relay_locations. The host SHOULD maintain relay connections to ensure the resource remains available to external peers. If no relay_locations are available, the resource is considered local-only.

ul.li: Public resources: Peers hosting public resources SHOULD ensure they are reachable via direct or relay connectivity
Private resources: Peers MAY restrict resources to local network or specific peer groups
Resource availability: Hosts SHOULD periodically refresh their resource announcements to maintain discoverability

section.t: Stale Discovery: Location hints in the DHT may become stale. A peer that cannot fetch a resource from a location hint MAY query the witness ring for the resource's current location or fall back to DHT re-resolution.
Cross-Verification: Implementations SHOULD cross-verify resource announcements with the witness ring before trusting location hints to prevent location spoofing attacks.
Quarantine and Discovery: If the governance primitive is supported, quarantined CIDs MUST NOT be returned in query responses. The error E_QUARANTINED (error code 0x10) SHOULD be returned instead.

0x10–0x1F: Governance, hash algorithm, NAT traversal, spillover, capability, and range errors
0x20–0x2F: Coral DHT errors

Both peers perform connectivity checks in priority order

Both peers discover witnesses via Coral DHT (LOOKUP_PATHS paths)
