section.name: Witness Ring Security Model
section.t: This section formalizes the security properties of QUIP's witness-ring mechanism — the distributed trust subsystem built on top of the Coral DHT's Kademlia XOR routing. It is organized as assumptions → adversary → goals → guarantees → failure bounds.

section.name: System Definition
section.t: A witness ring R(T, e) for target T at epoch e is the set of the WITNESS_COUNT = 7 closest reachable nodes to T in the 256-bit XOR-distance space, as discovered through LOOKUP_PATHS = 3 independent DHT paths with SPILLOVER_THRESHOLD = 2-of-3 consensus.

The ring provides one service: corroboration of Key Claims — transitioning an identity from PENDING (TOFU-only) to VERIFIED (witness-backed), and participating in full BFT consensus (5-of-7) for high-stakes operations: key rotation, revocation, witness membership changes, and ownership transfers.

tr.td: No domain, CA, or third-party trust is introduced
Architectural: all trust derives from TOFU + ring corroboration
The target's Ed25519 private key is uncompromised
Discrete-log hardness (RFC 8032); optionally hardened with FROST thresholds (t-of-n signing)
At most f = 2 ring members are Byzantine simultaneously
At most 1 of 3 lookup paths is attacker-controlled
LOOKUP_PATHS = 3, disjointness checked; else consensus threshold rises to 3-of-3
The peer performing the lookup is not compromised at first contact
Explicitly NOT assumed — see TOFU caveat,
Local clocks are within MAX_REPLAY_WINDOW (5 min)
Timestamp checks bound replay to a 5-minute window
Witness statements have bounded validity (24 h) and are re-issued at 12 h
Limits the value of a stolen witness key

section.name: Adversary Capabilities
section.t: The adversary can:

ul.li: Compromise or operate ≤ 2 witnesses in any single ring (e.g., via Sybil NodeIds).
Eavesdrop on all traffic (passive).
Control one DHT lookup path, including falsely rejecting witnesses to trigger spillover (up to 10/min/NodeId rate limit).
Maintain adversarial nodes online indefinitely, and pre-compute XOR-close NodeIds before an epoch (rotation does not force re-grinding in v1 — acknowledged in ).
Place infrastructure in the target's cluster region, reducing the effective search space in sparse deployments.
Inject false candidates, resource locations, connectivity announcements, or invalid Merkle range proofs.

section.t: The adversary cannot (assumed infeasible):

ul.li: Forge Ed25519 signatures or find SHA-256/BLAKE3 collisions.
Compromise the target NodeId's private key.
Control ≥ 3 witnesses in a ring — cost analysis in .
Control ≥ 2 disjoint lookup paths — requires XOR-close placement across disjoint node sets.
Produce a Merkle range proof that verifies against a BLAKE3 CID without holding the corresponding subtree.

section.name: Core Guarantee: Sybil Cost as the Safety Anchor
section.t: Claim 1 (Ring takeover infeasibility). Placing k nodes within T's 7-nearest-neighbor set requires finding NodeIds in a distance ball whose expected search cost is Θ(2²⁵⁶ / 2^d). For k = 3 (the minimum to break BFT safety), the adversary must simultaneously satisfy: (a) 3 XOR-close IDs, and (b) reachability/acceptance within the ring's filtering rules (recent liveness, ConnectivityAnnounce). Because the XOR metric has no exploitable structure, no shortcut exists — cost is linear in attempts, exactly the property that makes honest placement cheap and adversarial placement exponentially expensive.

Note on Mass Placement: The infeasibility argument assumes targeted placement near a specific target. An attacker who operates a large population of honest-looking nodes (e.g., a botnet) occupies a share of nearby slots proportional to their density. The XOR metric resists targeted placement, not mass placement. Whether at most 2 of the 7 witnesses are adversarial depends on network composition and is an environmental assumption (A3) that the protocol cannot verify. This is a documented limitation of the model.

Claim 2 (Quorum intersection). Any two BFT quorums of 5-of-7 intersect in ≥ 3 nodes. Since at most 2 are Byzantine, every quorum contains ≥ 3 honest members, and any two quorums share ≥ 1 honest member. This yields:

ul.li: Safety: no two conflicting operations (e.g., two rotations from the same old key) can both commit.
Consistency: a committed state is never overwritten by a conflicting one without detection.

section.t: Formally: for quorums Q₁, Q₂ ⊆ R, |Q₁| = |Q₂| = 5, |R| = 7 ⇒ |Q₁ ∩ Q₂| ≥ 3 > 2 = f.

tr.td: WitnessStatements signed per-witness; ring membership verified via cross-path consensus
VERIFIED status reflects ≥ 4 independent, live witnesses, each with claims first seen ≥ 6 h ago
Tolerates f = 2; below quorum, ring enters DEGRADED (3-of-4, f = 1) with critical ops queued
3 disjoint paths, 2-of-3 spillover consensus, PathProof signatures
One controlled path can delay but not corrupt; false rejection triggers spillover routing
Replays > 5 min old rejected; stale witnesses expire (E_WITNESS_EXPIRED)
DVV writes execute optimistically; BFT only on conflicts or critical ops
95% of writes skip consensus latency (< 5 ms target)

t.strong: Explicit non-goals (the ring does not provide):

ul.li: Absolute proof of real-world identity (VERIFIED is probabilistic, not CA-grade).
Protection against first-contact MITM (TOFU caveat).
Deletion/quarantine enforcement on nodes that opt out.
Within-epoch eviction of malicious witnesses (only epoch rotation resets membership).

tr.td: DEGRADED mode; critical ops deferred until 5-of-7 restored
Liveness trade-off: PENDING-status writes must await confirmation
Raise threshold to 3-of-3; fall back to cached witnesses
12 h re-issue interval bounds exposure; revocation tombstones propagate via gossip (5+ distinct reporters)

ol.li: Bootstrap (TOFU): first Key Claim pinned on sight. No ring protection yet — this is the one step resting on the transport channel alone.
Corroboration: ≥ 4 independent witnesses + ≥ 6 h elapsed → VERIFIED.
Operation: optimistic writes for eligible ops; full BFT for rotation/revocation/membership/transfer.
Repair: revocation via gossip tombstoning (5-of-n reporters) permanently downgrades to REVOKED — a one-way transition.

ul.li: TOFU window: an adversary controlling both the bootstrap view and first contact can substitute a key. The ring never recovers the wrong pin without out-of-band verification. Mitigation: OOB verification REQUIRED for high-security use; witness-ring diversity protects all subsequent contacts.
Sparse-region Sybil: with few honest nodes in a cluster, the effective placement cost drops. Mitigation: 3-path cross-validation, optional 9-witness rings.
Spillover DoS: bounded by rate limiting (10/min), PoW cost, response caching (5 min TTL), and exponential backoff.
Rotation without nonce-binding: adversary pre-positioned in epoch e remains in epoch e+1; takeover persists up to 24 h. Addressed in (nonce-bound epochs).

section.name: Model Verdict
section.t: The witness ring is a localized, cryptographically costed trust anchor. Its safety reduces to one clean argument — quorum intersection (5-of-7 intersecting in > f) — anchored by one clean assumption — that placing > 2 nodes in a ring is computationally infeasible via XOR-distance search. Everything else in the mechanism (paths, spillover, epochs, degradation ladder) exists to protect that one assumption from network-level and operational attacks.
The model's known soft spot is the TOFU first contact, which the protocol correctly refuses to overclaim. Without out-of-band verification, the witness ring cannot rescue a poisoned bootstrap.

The trust assumptions A3 (≤ 2 Byzantine witnesses) and A4 (≤ 1 attacker-controlled path) are environmental: the protocol can detect violations but cannot prove them. Deployments in sparse regions or adversarial network conditions SHOULD consider:

ul.li: Optional 9-witness rings (f=3) for higher security
Out-of-band bootstrap verification
Monitoring for eclipse and path-collusion attacks

section.name: Threat Model Summary
section.t: See for the detailed threat model and trust assumptions. The following subsections address specific operational and cryptographic security concerns.

section.name: NAT Traversal Security
section.t: Relay Security: Coral DHT relays are untrusted. All traffic through relays MUST be encrypted with the same QUIC+TLS 1.3 protection used for direct connections. Relays cannot decrypt or inspect traffic.

Relay DoS: Malicious peers could overload relays by requesting many connections. Relays SHOULD enforce rate limiting and connection caps. The RECOMMENDED rate limit is 100 connections per minute per NodeId.

NAT Spoofing: Peers could falsely advertise external addresses to misdirect traffic. Implementations SHOULD verify connectivity announcements through multiple DHT paths and SHOULD NOT trust unverified announcements.

section.name: Spillover Security
section.t: Spillover Abuse: Malicious peers could repeatedly trigger spillover to overwhelm the DHT. Implementations SHOULD rate-limit spillover requests to 10 per minute per NodeId.

Spillover Consensus: The 2-of-3 consensus threshold provides protection against path-based attacks. However, if an attacker controls 2 paths, they could force a false consensus. Implementations SHOULD monitor for path overlap and alert on suspicious patterns.

section.name: Hash Algorithm Security
section.t: SHA-256: SHA-256 is a NIST-approved hash function with no known practical collisions. It is the mandatory baseline for QUIP CIDs and provides 128 bits of post-quantum security.

BLAKE3: BLAKE3 is a modern hash function based on the BLAKE2/ChaCha architecture. It provides the same 256-bit security as SHA-256 and is considered secure for all cryptographic purposes. BLAKE3 is specified in the BLAKE3 specification . While BLAKE3 is not NIST-standardized, this is a deployment consideration rather than a security concern; the algorithm has been extensively cryptanalyzed and is widely deployed in production systems.

Algorithm Agility: Both algorithms produce the same digest size (32 bytes), enabling consistent CID handling regardless of which algorithm is used. The handshake extension hash_algo negotiates the algorithm. If no agreement is reached, peers MUST fall back to SHA-256.

Algorithm Downgrade Attacks: An adversary could attempt to force a downgrade to a weaker hash algorithm. Since both SHA-256 and BLAKE3 provide equivalent security levels (256-bit), this is not a concern. If future algorithms are added, implementations SHOULD require explicit opt-in for weaker algorithms.

CIDv1 Tagging: The OPTIONAL CIDv1 extension () prevents ambiguity across connections by including the hash algorithm in the identifier. Implementations MUST use CIDv1 for persistent state when both peers support it, as required by .

section.name: Merkle Range Fetching Security
section.t: Proof Forgery: A malicious responder could attempt to return bytes that do not match the requested range, accompanied by a forged proof. The client verifies the proof against the CID using BLAKE3's verification procedure; a forged proof is detected and rejected with E_PROOF_INVALID (error code 0x1C).

Range Amplification: A malicious requester could issue many small range requests to consume server CPU. Implementations SHOULD enforce per-NodeId rate limits on fetch_range as with other SYNC verbs, and SHOULD apply a per-connection byte-per-second cap independent of the number of requests.
Range Length Cap: MAX_RANGE_LENGTH bounds the memory cost of a single response. A responder MUST reject requests whose length exceeds the negotiated maximum with E_RANGE_INVALID (error code 0x1B).

Responder Tree Recomputation: A responder that does not have the chunk tree cached faces a CPU amplification risk if it recomputes the tree on every fetch_range request, because recomputation is O(resource_size) while a request is O(1) in size. Implementations that choose to recompute on demand MUST rate-limit such requests or cache the tree after first recomputation. Implementations that cannot bound the recomputation cost SHOULD reject such requests with E_RANGE_INVALID (error code 0x1B).

Timing Side Channels: Merkle range fetching reveals which portions of a resource a peer is interested in. This is inherent to any partial retrieval scheme and is equivalent to the information revealed by HTTP Range requests. Deployments that require access-pattern privacy SHOULD use full-resource downloads instead.

Interaction with Quarantine: Range fetching is subject to the same quarantine policy as other reads. A quarantined CID MUST NOT be served via range_response, even if the requester knows the exact CID. Implementations SHOULD reject such requests with E_QUARANTINED (error code 0x10).

section.name: Operational Security Considerations
section.t: Implementations face operational denial-of-service risks from resource exhaustion. The following bounds are RECOMMENDED defaults; deployments MAY tune them for their environment.

figure.artwork: DoS Mitigation (RECOMMENDED defaults): - Per-NodeId rate limiting: 1000 ops/min - Per-connection max streams: 256 - Max message size: 64 KB - Witness ring capacity: MAX_CAPACITY = 10 pending rings - Backoff on repeated errors: exponential, capped at 60s - Pin announcements: 100/min per NodeId - Max pins per peer: 1000 - RBSR max ranges: 1024 per request - Governance operations: 100/min per NodeId (if supported) - Spillover requests: 10/min per NodeId - Relay connections: 100/min per NodeId - Range request bytes served: 64 MB/min per connection (if supported) - Range tree recomputation: rate-limited per NodeId (if recompute-on-demand)

section.t: Rate Limiting: Peers SHOULD enforce a per-NodeId limit of 1000 operations per minute on T0 and T1 traffic. Requests beyond this limit MUST be rejected with E_RATE_LIMIT (error code 0x03), with a short burst allowance (RECOMMENDED: 100 operations) to absorb legitimate bursts.

Memory Bounds: A single QUIP message MUST NOT exceed 64 KB (see the max_message_size handshake extension in ); oversized messages MUST be rejected with E_BAD_ENCODING. Implementations SHOULD bound per-connection memory use to a small, fixed multiple of this limit. Range responses that exceed the per-message cap MUST be split across multiple fetch_range requests.

Connection Throttling: A peer SHOULD limit concurrent T2 (BULK) streams per connection to 256 and SHOULD apply exponential backoff after repeated protocol errors from the same NodeId, capped at 60 seconds (1 minute) between retries.

Witness Ring Load: A witness SHOULD cap the number of rings it actively participates in (MAX_CAPACITY = 10) to bound the cost of BFT consensus participation, and MAY decline new ring assignments once at capacity.
Pin Flooding: Peers SHOULD limit pin announcements to 100 per minute per NodeId to prevent DoS. A peer MAY ignore pins from unverified NodeIds.
CID Collision Resistance: SHA-256 and BLAKE3 are assumed collision-resistant. Implementations SHOULD reject CIDs that do not match the payload hash with error E_CID_MISMATCH (error code 0x0C).
Resource Exhaustion via Pinning: Implementations SHOULD limit the number of pinned resources per peer to 1000. The pin_capacity handshake extension () can be used to advertise capacity.

RBSR Range Attacks: A malicious peer could request many small ranges to cause CPU exhaustion. Implementations SHOULD limit RBSR requests to 1024 ranges (max_ranges handshake extension) and impose per-request computational limits.

Resource Discovery Attacks: A malicious peer MAY announce false resource locations to redirect traffic. Implementations SHOULD cross-verify resource announcements with the witness ring before trusting location hints. The error E_RESOURCE_STALE (error code 0x0F) is provided for stale discovery handling.

Content Poisoning: A malicious peer could announce a resource with a valid CID but serve malicious bytes. CID verification at fetch time catches this: the fetched payload MUST match the CID. To mitigate discovery-layer poisoning, implementations SHOULD fetch from multiple locations and compare CIDs before accepting content.

section.name: Governance Primitive Security
section.t: False Governance Attacks: An adversary could submit false quarantine requests. Mitigations include:

ul.li: Witness ring validation (5 of 7 witnesses required)
Application-defined evidence requirements
Audit trails for all governance operations
Quarantine expiration (applications SHOULD set reasonable TTLs)
Rate limiting of governance operations (RECOMMENDED: 100/min per NodeId)

section.t: Delegation Abuse: Stolen or compromised NodeIds could be used to issue governance operations. Mitigations include:

ul.li: Short-lived delegation certificates
Revocation capability for delegates
Witness ring validation of delegate authority
Application-defined permission bits

section.t: Quarantine Evasion: Content can be modified to evade detection. This is a fundamental limitation. Applications SHOULD use multiple detection mechanisms and maintain escalation paths for manual review.
Privacy Implications: Governance metadata (perceptual hashes, evidence) may reveal content characteristics. Applications SHOULD consider privacy implications when designing governance policies.
DoS via Quarantine: An adversary could submit many quarantine requests. Implementations SHOULD rate-limit governance operations and require witness ring validation to prevent abuse.

section.name: Sybil Attack Analysis
section.t: XOR Distance Search Problem: Given a target NodeId T, finding a NodeId N such that distance(T, N) < d is a search problem over the 32-byte space. The XOR metric provides no exploitable structure; the expected number of attempts to find a node within distance d is O(2^256 / 2^d).

For the 7-nearest-neighbor set, d is such that the expected number of attempts is approximately 2^256 / 2^(256/7) ≈ 2^220. This figure is illustrative and depends on network size and adversary distribution. A discussion of quantitative models for Kademlia Sybil resistance can be found in , .

Mass Placement vs. Targeted Placement: The analysis above applies to targeted placement near a specific target. An attacker operating a large honest-looking node population (e.g., a botnet) occupies a share of nearby slots proportional to their density. The XOR metric does not protect against mass placement; it only makes targeted placement expensive. This is an environmental assumption (A3 in ) that the protocol cannot verify.

Relationship to Witness Constants: The cost analysis justifies the choice of f=2 (7 witnesses) in . Controlling 3+ witnesses in a ring is computationally infeasible for targeted attacks; mass attacks depend on network composition.

Multiple Paths and Sybil Attacks: The Coral DHT's multiple lookup paths make Sybil attacks more expensive. An attacker must control nodes on multiple paths to successfully corrupt witness discovery. This multiplies the cost of Sybil attacks by a factor of LOOKUP_PATHS (3). However, under eclipse/bootstrap-poisoning attacks, all three paths may be attacker-controlled while remaining disjoint — see for the full discussion.

section.name: Impact of Coral DHT Clustering on Witness Selection and Sybil Resistance
section.t: The introduction of Coral DHT clustering (described in ) adds a locality-based component to witness discovery. This raises a question: does the RTT-based clustering affect the Sybil resistance of the witness ring selection?

Clustering as a Performance Optimization: In QUIP, Coral DHT clustering is used primarily as a performance optimization for routing and NAT traversal. The fundamental witness selection mechanism remains based on the Kademlia XOR distance metric, as specified in . Specifically:

ul.li: The 7 closest (by XOR distance) reachable nodes are chosen as the witness ring.

Clustering is used to accelerate lookups and to filter candidates for reachability (e.g., via ConnectivityAnnounce), but it does NOT modify the XOR distance calculation or the rule that the nearest nodes form the ring.
Therefore, the Sybil resistance analysis in , which relies on the computational cost of generating XOR-close NodeIds, remains valid for targeted attacks.

section.t: Attack Scenario with Clustering: An adversary with resources in a target region could attempt a Sybil attack by generating NodeIds that are XOR-close to the target and also satisfy the cluster acceptance criteria (i.e., are reachable within the cluster's RTT bound). This reduces the effective search space: the attacker must find NodeIds that are not only XOR-close but also network-proximate to the target region.

Quantitative Analysis: The reduction in search space depends on the geographic distribution of honest nodes and the attacker's ability to place infrastructure in the target cluster. In a dense global network, the attacker's ability to influence the ring is still dominated by the XOR distance search cost. In sparse regional deployments (e.g., early adoption with a few hundred nodes in a region), the pool of honest nodes is smaller, which could make a Sybil attack more feasible. Implementations in such environments SHOULD consider:

ul.li: Requiring a larger witness count (e.g., 9) for high-security applications.
Monitoring cluster-merge attacks as described in .
Cross-validating witness rings from multiple Coral DHT lookups (as already required by the LOOKUP_PATHS and spillover mechanisms).

section.t: Conclusion: In the current design, clustering does not weaken the fundamental Sybil resistance of the XOR distance metric, because witness eligibility remains purely based on XOR distance. However, network sparsity can reduce the effective effort for an attacker to place a node within the nearest-neighbor set. This is a known limitation of any geographically-aware DHT and is addressed through the protocol's existing mitigation mechanisms (multiple paths, spillover, and the optional larger witness count). A full quantitative treatment of Sybil resistance in the Coral DHT model is deferred to future work.

section.name: A.1 Coral DHT Implementation
section.t: Implementations MAY use any Coral DHT implementation (e.g., libp2p Coral DHT, custom implementation, or adaptation of existing Kademlia implementations). The protocol specifies the Kademlia XOR distance metric, witness selection algorithm, multiple lookup paths, and spillover mechanisms.

ol.li: Implementations SHOULD ship with at least 5 bootstrap nodes hardcoded or configurable.
Coral DHT bootstrap nodes SHOULD be geographically diverse to enable proper clustering. New peers SHOULD bootstrap from multiple clusters to get a balanced view of the network.
Bootstrap nodes are NOT trusted parties — they are used only to obtain an initial set of DHT contacts. They MUST NOT be treated as witnesses or authorities.

section.t: Malicious Bootstrap Node Mitigations: A malicious bootstrap node can only supply a biased initial contact list. However, if multiple bootstrap nodes are compromised, they could partition new peers. Implementations SHOULD:

ul.li: Cross-validate bootstrap responses: compare contacts from different bootstrap nodes and flag inconsistencies
Use a diverse set of bootstrap nodes from different autonomous systems and jurisdictions
Maintain a persisted routing table from previous sessions as a fallback
If bootstrap nodes consistently return different routing table views, enter "split-brain" detection mode and alert the user

section.t: Bootstrap Diversity Requirement: Implementations SHOULD maintain a list of at least 5 bootstrap nodes operated by independent entities. The list SHOULD be configurable by the user to allow alternative bootstrap paths in case of censorship or compromise.

No Bootstrap Nodes Available: If a peer cannot reach any configured bootstrap node, it SHOULD fall back to any DHT contacts learned from prior sessions (a persisted routing table), and MAY use local network discovery (e.g., mDNS) to find peers who can supply DHT contacts. A peer that cannot join the DHT by any means MUST treat all Key Claims as PENDING until DHT connectivity is established, since witness verification is not possible without it.

Bootstrap Security: Because bootstrap nodes are untrusted, a compromised or malicious bootstrap node can at most supply a biased initial contact list. However, if an adversary controls the bootstrap AND intercepts the first contact, they can direct the peer to a Sybil-dominated DHT view. Normal Kademlia routing and witness diversity () mitigate this after the peer has established multiple independent DHT connections. Out-of-band verification of the initial Key Claim is REQUIRED to eliminate this vector.

Persisted Routing Table: Implementations SHOULD persist DHT routing table state between sessions to reduce reliance on bootstrap nodes and improve startup time. Persisted contacts MUST be validated before use (e.g., by checking that they are still reachable and have not expired).

ol.li: Each lookup path uses a different set of DHT nodes
Path selection SHOULD be deterministic to enable verification
Path diversity SHOULD be maximized (nodes from different clusters)
Implementations SHOULD verify path independence

section.name: A.2 RBSR Implementation
section.t: Implementations MAY choose from several fingerprint algorithms:

ul.li: Algo 0 (XOR): MUST be implemented. Simple XOR of range hashes. Fast but collision-prone for very large sets. This is the baseline and fallback algorithm.
Algo 1 (IBLT): MAY be implemented. Invertible Bloom Lookup Tables. Efficient for set differences but more complex. Suitable for large datasets with small diffs.
Algo 2 (Merkle): MAY be implemented. Merkle tree roots. Highest security but highest overhead. Suitable for security-critical datasets.
XOR: Use for most applications. Fastest, sufficient for typical sync workloads.
IBLT: Use when diff is small relative to total set (e.g., 1% change in a 1GB dataset).
Merkle: Use when security/verification is critical (e.g., financial data, code repositories).

section.t: Range Size Selection: Implementations SHOULD choose range sizes based on expected data size and network conditions. Typical values:

ul.li: Small documents (<1MB): 1 range (entire document)
Medium documents (1-100MB): 64KB-1MB ranges
Large datasets (>100MB): 1-16MB ranges

section.t: Fingerprint Caching: Implementations SHOULD cache fingerprints for frequently-synced resources to avoid recomputation.
Algorithm Negotiation: Peers SHOULD negotiate the fingerprint algorithm via the rbsr_algo handshake extension (0x08). If no agreement is reached, the peer MUST fall back to XOR (algo=0).

section.name: A.3 CID Implementation
section.t: QUIP uses a simplified CID format: raw hash digest (32 bytes). This is equivalent to the multihash encoding without the multicodec prefix.

ul.li: Available in all standard libraries
FIPS-compliant
Requires BLAKE3 library (blake3 crate in Rust, blake3 npm package in JavaScript)
Not FIPS-compliant

section.t: CIDv1 Implementation: When both peers support CIDv1 (bit 9 in capabilities), implementations MUST use the tagged format for persistent state:

ul.li: hash_algo = 0 for SHA-256, 1 for BLAKE3
CIDv1 MUST be used for pins, quarantine, governance, and any state that persists across connections

section.t: CID in DVV: The CID in the Dot struct () references the same CID as the corresponding set operation. This ensures that the DVV state is content-addressable and enables CAS (compare-and-swap) operations.
Hash Algorithm Negotiation: Peers SHOULD negotiate the hash algorithm via the hash_algo handshake extension. If no agreement is reached, the peer MUST fall back to SHA-256 (algo=0).

ul.li: BLAKE3 is approximately 3× faster than SHA-256 for large data
BLAKE3 supports parallel execution on multi-core systems
BLAKE3's tree structure enables partial verification
BLAKE3 includes built-in key derivation (derive_key)

section.name: A.4 Merkle Range Fetching Implementation
section.t: BLAKE3 Library Support: BLAKE3 libraries that support the verified streaming API (e.g., the Rust blake3 crate's Hasher and ChunkState types, or the official reference implementations) provide the primitive operations needed to build and verify range proofs. Implementations SHOULD use a library with native support rather than reimplementing the tree structure.

Chunk Alignment: Range requests are not required to be chunk-aligned. The responder SHOULD compute the smallest set of BLAKE3 subtrees that covers the requested range and return a proof composed of the sibling chaining values along the path to the root. Non-aligned ranges may require the responder to return a slightly larger set of leaf chunks than the request strictly specifies; the wire response still contains exactly the requested bytes plus the proof.

Proof Size: The proof size is proportional to log2(resource_size / chunk_size) × 32 bytes plus the size of the covering subtree's chaining values. For a 1 GiB resource and a 64 KiB range, the proof is on the order of a few kilobytes. This is small relative to the transferred bytes for any reasonable range length.

Range Length Trade-off: Small ranges (below BLAKE3_CHUNK_SIZE × 8 or so) pay a proportionally larger proof overhead. Implementations SHOULD prefer ranges of at least 8 KiB to amortize proof cost, and MAY batch multiple small logical ranges into a single physical request when the caller controls the request granularity.

Responder State: The responder needs the resource's chunk tree to construct proofs. Implementations SHOULD cache the tree alongside the blob when the resource is written with merkle_range enabled. If the tree is not cached, the responder faces a choice: recompute the tree from the blob on demand, or reject the request with E_RANGE_INVALID (error code 0x1B). Recomputation is O(resource_size) per request and can be exploited for CPU amplification; a responder that chooses to recompute SHOULD rate-limit recomputation per NodeId and SHOULD cache the tree after the first recomputation so that subsequent requests are O(log(resource_size)). A responder that cannot bound the recomputation cost SHOULD reject the request rather than recompute.
Client Verification: The client MUST run the full BLAKE3 verification procedure against the CID, not merely check the proof's structure. Structural checks alone do not detect adversarial proofs.

Quarantine Integration: When the governance primitive is supported, the responder MUST apply the same quarantine policy to range responses as to whole-resource reads. A quarantined CID is not served via fetch_range, regardless of what range is requested.

section.name: A.5 NAT Traversal Implementation
section.t: DHT Address Discovery: Implementations SHOULD discover external addresses using Coral DHT peers rather than STUN. A peer SHOULD request address observations from multiple independent DHT peers, verify the returned observations, and use the most consistent external address. Implementations MUST NOT require STUN or any centralized address-discovery service.
NAT Type Detection: NAT type detection SHOULD use Coral DHT connectivity probes from multiple independent peers. The RECOMMENDED approach is:

ol.li: Send connectivity probes from 3 distinct Coral DHT peers
Compare observed addresses from different sources

li.t: Infer NAT type from consistency of observed addresses:

ul.li: All same: open or cone NAT
Different ports, same IP: restricted cone NAT
Different IPs: symmetric NAT

section.t: Relay Discovery Correlation: Implementations that issue multiple concurrent relay_discovery requests MUST generate a fresh, unique request_id for each and match responses by both request_id and target. Implementations MUST NOT rely on arrival order or on the target field alone to demultiplex responses. See .

Relay-hop HPKE: Implementations that emit or consume multi-hop relay chains MUST implement the HPKE suite defined in : DHKEM(X25519, HKDF-SHA256) / HKDF-SHA256 / ChaCha20Poly1305, with info = "QUIP-relay-hop-v1" and empty aad. The Ed25519-to-X25519 birational map used to derive the recipient public key is available in every mainstream cryptographic library (libsodium's crypto_sign_ed25519_pk_to_curve25519, Go's filippo.io/edwards25519 together with x/crypto/curve25519, Rust's curve25519-dalek together with ed25519-dalek, and the reference HPKE implementations). Implementations SHOULD NOT roll their own birational map; use the library-provided one and verify it against the RFC 8032 test vectors.
Relay Selection: When selecting relays, implementations SHOULD consider:

ul.li: XOR distance to the target (prefer closer relays)
Available capacity (prefer less loaded relays)
Geographic proximity (if available from cluster info)
Historical reliability (prefer relays with good uptime)

section.t: Connectivity Checks: Implementations SHOULD perform connectivity checks in parallel to minimize latency. The RECOMMENDED timeout for connectivity checks is 5 seconds.
Fallback Behavior: If all connectivity checks fail, implementations SHOULD:

ol.li: Retry with different relay nodes
Use additional Coral DHT relays or cached relay entries if available
Enter DEGRADED mode with reduced functionality

section.name: A.6 Pinning Implementation
section.t: Local Pinning: Peers SHOULD store pinned resources until the TTL expires. Resources with ttl=0 select the default TTL (RECOMMENDED: 7 days / 604800 seconds); resources with ttl=0xFFFFFFFF are stored indefinitely (subject to storage capacity).
Pin Propagation: Peers SHOULD announce pins via T3 pin_announce messages. The witness signature provides credibility to the pin request.
Pin Refreshing: Peers SHOULD refresh pins before TTL expiry (at 80% of TTL) to maintain persistence.
Pin Eviction: When storage capacity is reached, peers SHOULD evict pins with the lowest ref_count or oldest pinned_at timestamp.

Pin Verification: A pin is a signed promise, not a verified delivery receipt. Deployments requiring stronger guarantees MAY layer independent retrievability challenges (e.g., periodic fetch-and-verify probes by third parties, publicly logged) on top of the pin primitive.

section.name: A.7 Resource Discovery Implementation
section.t: Announcement Frequency: Peers SHOULD re-announce resources every 24 hours (with ±1 hour jitter to avoid announcement storms) or whenever the CID changes.
Stale Locations: A peer that cannot fetch a resource from a location hint MAY query the witness ring for the resource's current location or fall back to DHT re-resolution.
Cross-Verification: Implementations SHOULD cross-verify resource announcements with the witness ring before trusting location hints to prevent location spoofing attacks.

section.name: A.8 Governance Implementation
section.t: Trusted CID Registration: Implementations SHOULD verify that the CID in the registration matches the content referenced. Implementations MAY verify application-defined metadata (e.g., perceptual hashes).
Quarantine Storage: Implementations SHOULD store quarantine state in persistent storage to survive restarts. Quarantine notices SHOULD be gossiped to ensure consistency across the network.

Derivative Detection: Applications SHOULD use multiple perceptual hash algorithms to reduce false positives. A RECOMMENDED approach is to require agreement between two algorithms (e.g., pHash and dHash) before marking content as a derivative.
Governance Rate Limiting: Implementations SHOULD limit governance operations to 100 per minute per NodeId to prevent DoS.

section.name: A.9 Test Vectors
section.t: Formal test vectors for all message types, DVV merge scenarios, the signing convention of (including at least one self-signed message, one witness-signed message, one IndividualRingSig, and one FrostRingSig), CID generation (SHA-256 and BLAKE3), CIDv1 tagging, pinning operations, resource discovery, NAT traversal, spillover, governance primitives, BFT consensus with checkpointing and ring signatures, and Merkle range proofs will be published at <https://github.com/jjmututi/quip-test-vectors> prior to the reference implementation release.

The relay-hop test vectors cover at least: a single-hop relay chain, a two-hop relay chain (the RELAY_HOP_LIMIT maximum), a chain whose first-hop HPKE ciphertext has been tampered with (must fail to open), a chain whose sender signature has been stripped (must fail to verify), and a chain whose HPKE info string is the wrong length (must fail to open).

The Merkle range test vectors cover at least: a range aligned to BLAKE3's native chunk boundaries, a range unaligned on both ends, a range covering the entire resource, a range of length 1 byte, a proof that fails verification against a mismatched CID, and a request served by a responder that recomputed the chunk tree on demand rather than from cache.

Implementers SHOULD run the signing test vectors against their implementation before deployment; signing payload mismatches are a common source of silent interoperability failure and will not be caught by generic CBOR conformance tests. The Merkle range test vectors should be run against any implementation that advertises merkle_range.

section.name: Appendix B: Why QUIP, Why Now
section.t: QUIP combines several existing primitives into a coherent federation protocol: QUIC transport, Ed25519 self-sovereign identity, Dotted Version Vectors, Coral DHT-based witness discovery, NAT traversal, explicit backpressure, and (optionally) BLAKE3 Merkle range fetching. None of these primitives are new. Their composition is.

t.strong: Why this composition did not exist earlier:

ul.li: Browser-centric standards froze the transport layer: QUIC was standardized for HTTP/3; raw QUIC with application-defined streams and flow control was treated as an implementation detail.
Identity models remained domain-bound: Federation protocols typically delegated to OAuth/OIDC brokers or adopted domain-based DANE, introducing third-party dependencies.
Database techniques stayed inside databases: Dotted Version Vectors were not exposed as a wire primitive.
Infrastructure incentives rewarded buffering: RAM was cheap, so hidden buffering was tolerated.
NAT traversal was centralized: STUN/TURN required centralized servers; Coral DHT enables decentralized NAT traversal.

Range retrieval was HTTP-shaped: Byte ranges were treated as a transport-layer concern rather than a content-layer concern; BLAKE3's tree structure makes verifiable range retrieval a property of the content, not the transport.
Regulatory pressure: The EU Digital Markets Act requires gatekeepers to support third-party federation.
Cost pressure: AI inference and real-time applications make RAM and tail latency first-order costs.
Implementation maturity: Production QUIC stacks are stable and support datagrams.
Existence proof: Mastodon and Bluesky proved users want federation.
DHT maturity: Coral DHT has been proven in production deployments (e.g., Coral CDN, libp2p).
Hash maturity: BLAKE3 has reached production stability with native support for verified streaming, making Merkle range fetching a wire-format decision rather than a cryptographic research problem.

section.t: Why unification matters: The current separation of DNS (identity), HTTP (transport), and content storage is a historical artifact of centralization, not a law of nature. In a decentralized system, there is no domain owner to serve as the authority linking identity to content. QUIP provides an alternative architecture where identity and content are coupled through cryptographic verification, and where range-level access to content is a property of the content itself.

section.name: Appendix C: Why Not Existing Solutions
section.t: This appendix addresses common comparisons to existing federation and P2P systems (non-normative):

tr.td: Hidden buffering behind HTTP semantics; typically paired with OAuth/IdP-based identity, which QUIP eliminates. Range requests are transport-layer only, unverifiable against content identity.
Pubsub delivery is not reliable enough for causal consistency; no built-in causality primitive. Range retrieval is defined at the block layer, not the resource layer.
Not designed for real-time delivery; no explicit backpressure or transport tiers; no range retrieval.
Requires centralized signaling servers; no built-in identity or DHT discovery
Protocol framework, not a specific protocol; QUIP defines a complete federation protocol

section.name: Appendix D: Future Work
section.t: The following extensions are under consideration for a future version of this document and are not part of this specification:

ul.li: MST (Merkle Search Tree)-based sync: Alternative sync optimization using Merkle search trees for large datasets.
Ring-based grouping: For high-fanout power users, allowing them to maintain multiple witness rings for different purposes.
Privacy-preserving witness discovery: Hiding the target NodeId from the DHT during lookup through oblivious routing or private information retrieval.
Privacy-preserving range fetching: Oblivious Merkle range retrieval that hides which byte ranges are being requested from the responder.
Hardware acceleration: Optional integration with hardware security modules for threshold signature operations.
Payment/channel incentives: Micro-payments for pinning and storage using lightning or other payment channels.

Retrievability proofs: Verifying a pinner actually holds the bytes, not just that they signed a promise to. BLAKE3's tree structure makes partial retrievability proofs cheaper than they would be for SHA-256.
SHA-256 range fetching via RFC 6962 construction: A Merkle-over-SHA-256 construction defined at the QUIP layer that mirrors RFC 6962's tree shape, for deployments that cannot adopt BLAKE3.
Multi-algorithm range proofs: Allowing a single resource to be range-fetchable under multiple hash algorithms by publishing parallel proofs.
Variable witness counts: Support for 5-witness rings (low-power devices) or 9-witness rings (high-security environments).
Nonce-bound epoch rotation: Cryptographically binding witnesses to a specific epoch using a random nonce, preventing pre-computation of witness positions across epochs.

Content Governance Enhancements: Perceptual hash standardization, dispute resolution mechanisms, automated content moderation integration. The core primitives (Trusted CIDs, quarantine, derivative linking) are included in version 03; the enhancements listed here are for future consideration.
Additional Hash Algorithms: Support for BLAKE3 is included in version 03; additional algorithms may be added in future versions as they become standardized.
Path diversity optimization: Adaptive path selection based on network conditions and attack patterns.

section.t: RBSR is now included in the base specification as of version 03 and is no longer considered future work. Merkle range fetching is included in version 03 as an OPTIONAL capability; future versions may extend it as noted above.

section.name: Appendix E: Implementation Status
section.t: This section records the status of known implementations at the time of writing, per the guidance of . It will be removed before publication as an RFC.

tr.td: Core + RBSR + CID (SHA-256 + BLAKE3) + CIDv1 + Pinning + Governance + Resource Discovery + NAT Traversal + Coral DHT + Spillover + BFT Checkpointing + Ring Signatures + Merkle Range Fetching
Core + CID (SHA-256) + CIDv1 + Pinning + Resource Discovery + NAT Traversal (basic)
Core + WebTransport + CID (SHA-256 + BLAKE3) + CIDv1 + NAT Traversal (via WebRTC) + Merkle Range Fetching
Core + CID (SHA-256 + BLAKE3) + CIDv1 + Governance + NAT Traversal (via WebTransport) + Merkle Range Fetching

ul.li: Core Protocol: Rust reference implementation targeting Q4 2026. Go and Python implementations planned for 2027.
RBSR Extension: Rust implementation planned with XOR (MUST) and IBLT (OPTIONAL) fingerprints. Go implementation to follow.

CID Extension: All implementations will support SHA-256 CIDs. BLAKE3 support is OPTIONAL and planned for Rust and JavaScript implementations. CIDv1 tagging is required for all implementations that support persistent state.

Merkle Range Extension: Rust and JavaScript implementations planned. Requires a BLAKE3 library with verified streaming support. Implementations that do not enable merkle_range remain fully protocol-compliant.
Pinning Extension: Rust and Go implementations planned. T3 pin_announce gossip to be included in all implementations.
Governance Extension: Rust implementation planned with Trusted CIDs, quarantine, and derivative linking. Go implementation to follow in 2027.
Resource Discovery: Rust implementation planned with resource_announce and query_resource. Go implementation to follow.
NAT Traversal: Rust implementation planned with Coral DHT-assisted NAT traversal. Go implementation to follow.
Coral DHT + Spillover: Rust implementation planned with 3 lookup paths and spillover mechanism.
BFT Checkpointing + Ring Signatures: Rust implementation planned with checkpoint interval 100, VIEW_CHANGE_QUORUM = 5, and both individual and FROST ring signature support.
Signing Convention: All implementations will follow the signing convention in . The Rust reference implementation will provide the canonical test vectors described in .
WebTransport: JavaScript implementation targeting 2027 Q3, enabling browser-based QUIP clients.

section.t: Interested implementers should contact the author for coordination and to ensure compatibility across implementations.

Test Vectors: Formal test vectors for all message types, DVV merge scenarios, the signing convention (), CID generation (SHA-256 and BLAKE3), CIDv1 tagging, pinning operations, resource discovery, NAT traversal, spillover, governance primitives, BFT consensus with checkpointing and ring signatures, and Merkle range proofs will be published at <https://github.com/jjmututi/quip-test-vectors> prior to the reference implementation release.

Interoperability Testing: A plugfest is planned for 2027 Q2 to test interoperability between Rust, Go, and Python implementations, including Merkle range fetching between implementations that advertise merkle_range. Details will be announced on the QUIP mailing list.

section.name: Appendix F: Performance Expectations (Non-Normative)
section.t: These figures are targets based on typical deployment scenarios and are not conformance requirements:

ul.li: Optimistic write (no conflict): <5ms under ideal conditions
BFT consensus (on conflict): <50ms under ideal conditions
Sync: O(diff), not O(total state)
Memory per connection: <1MB typical
Max concurrent streams per connection: 256 (configurable)
SHA-256 CID generation: ~2.3 GiB/s typical
BLAKE3 CID generation: ~5.2 GiB/s typical (3× faster)
Coral DHT lookup (3 paths): <200ms typical (with local caching)
Coral DHT lookup (3 paths, cold cache): <500ms typical
Spillover resolution: <500ms typical (when triggered)
NAT hole punching: <500ms typical
Relay connection establishment: <1s typical
Coral DHT cluster formation: <5s typical (for joining peers)
Coral DHT cluster maintenance: <100ms per heartbeat
Merkle range fetch (1 MiB range, warm cache): <50ms typical
Merkle range proof verification: <10ms typical for a 1 MiB range in a 1 GiB resource
Path count: LOOKUP_PATHS (3) increases lookup bandwidth by 3× but provides resilience benefits
Clustering: Clustering reduces lookup latency for local peers by 50-80%
Cache hierarchy: Coral's cache hierarchy reduces lookup latency for popular resources by 80-95%
Network size: Performance scales logarithmically with network size (O(log n) lookups)
Range length: Proof size scales logarithmically with resource size; the proof overhead amortizes better over larger ranges

Chunk tree caching: Responders that cache the chunk tree avoid recomputation on each request; this reduces per-request cost from O(resource_size) to O(log(resource_size)). Responders that do not cache the tree incur recomputation cost per request and should rate-limit accordingly.

Parallel requests: A client fetching a large resource can issue multiple range requests in parallel; the per-request overhead is dominated by the proof size, not by the payload size, for ranges above roughly 8 KiB

section.t: Actual performance depends on network conditions, hardware, deployment scale, and the specific operations being performed. Implementers SHOULD measure performance under their specific deployment conditions rather than relying on these illustrative figures.
